feed.title: Strokkur geyser, Haukadalur

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Strokkur, Icelandic for "churn", is a fountain-type geyser in a geothermal area beside the Hvítá River in the southwest of Iceland, east of Reykjavík. It typically erupts every 6–10 minutes. Its usual height is 15–20 metres, although it can sometimes erupt up to 40 metres high. Diego Delso photographed it on 16 August 2014 at 13:21, in hard midday light. The Commons description places the frame in the Haukadalur geothermal area. In this tall vertical, a small group of visitors in bright jackets stands on the pale ground at the lower right, with the turquoise water of the basin domed in front of them.
feed.lookAt: Almost the whole tall frame is empty blue sky with one white cloud, while a few figures in bright jackets sit tiny at the bottom beside the domed pool. The people give scale and the sky gives calm. Shoot vertically, keep the horizon low, and compose before the water rises.

feed.title: Jintai Temple, Zhuhai

image.credit: Dllu, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Southern slopes of the second peak of Huangyang Mountain

feed.story: Jintai Temple, written 金臺寺 in traditional characters and pronounced Jīn Tái Sì, is a temple complex on the southern slopes of the second peak of Huangyang Mountain in Doumen District, Zhuhai City, Guangdong Province. Dllu photographed it on 8 January 2024 at about 17:17 from across the water, and the Commons title calls it a remote view. Orange tiled roofs and yellow halls sit high on a forested hillside, while a long bridge runs through the trees below and a band of turquoise water fills the bottom of the frame.
feed.lookAt: From across the water, the orange roofs and yellow halls look small against a huge green hillside. A distant view lets you show a building in its setting. Use a longer lens to compress the slope, and let the dark trees and the turquoise water frame the bright roofs.

feed.title: Unemployed lumber worker, Oregon

image.credit: Dorothea Lange, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Dorothea Lange (1895–1965) was an American documentary photographer best known for her Depression-era work for the Farm Security Administration. Her photographs, the article says, humanized the consequences of the Great Depression. The caption for this August 1939 picture reads: unemployed lumber worker goes with his wife to the bean harvest, with a social security number tattooed on his arm, in Oregon. It is held by the Library of Congress under the digital ID fsa.8b15572. The man sits shirtless on a block of wood with a pipe in his mouth, facing the camera, while his wife sits behind him at the left inside a tent of hanging cloth.
feed.lookAt: A man sits close to the camera and looks at it, and his wife sits farther back, turned away inside a tent of cloth. Putting two people at different distances tells the story of the place without a word. Come in at eye level, ask for the stare, and let the background stay simple.

feed.title: Kaikōura Ranges from Mt Fyffe trail

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Seen from a great distance, including the North Island's southern coast

feed.story: The Kaikōura Ranges are two parallel ranges of mountains in the Canterbury Region, in the northeast of New Zealand's South Island. The two ranges are visible from a great distance, including from the southern coast of the North Island. Michal Klajban took this picture on 20 October 2019 at about 10:20 in the morning, from the trail to Mt Fyffe. The Commons description says it shows the Kowhai River at the bottom, with the ranges west of Mt Fyffe beyond it. In the wide frame, steep green slopes drop toward a pale strip of riverbed, and snow lies along the high ridgeline under thin streaks of cloud.
feed.lookAt: Dark scrub frames the left and right edges, and the eye slides down the green slopes to a pale ribbon of riverbed before climbing to the snowy ridge. Stand where the foreground can act as a frame, and use a wide crop so the ranges feel long and layered.

caption.title: Kaikōura Ranges from Mt Fyffe trail

feed.title: City pillar shrine, Phayao

image.credit: BigDom, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: On the shore of Phayao Lake
As a city-state about 900–1,000 years ago

feed.story: Phayao is a city in northern Thailand and the capital of Phayao Province. The town lies on the shore of Phayao Lake, and the Wikipedia article says it dates back to a semi-independent city-state founded between 900 and 1,000 years ago. It lies 726 km north of Bangkok. BigDom photographed the tree-lined walkway leading to the north facade of the city pillar, or lak mueang, shrine on 24 January 2024 at about 16:54. A small white shrine with a stepped spire stands at the end of a paved path, framed by tall trees with orange garlands at its steps.
feed.lookAt: A paved path runs between two trees to a small white shrine, and the branches arch overhead like a frame. Stand on the centre line to make the scene symmetrical. Keep the shrine small and leave space around it so the trees and sky do the framing.

feed.title: Freight train near Laguna, New Mexico

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano (1914–1997) was a Russian Empire-born photographer, filmmaker and composer who worked for the Farm Security Administration. The Library of Congress catalogues this colour transparency, dated March 1943, as a freight train stopping for coal and water at a siding en route to Gallup, New Mexico, near Laguna. Delano shot it from above the cars, looking along the roofs of the train toward the front. Beyond the tracks, a coaling tower sends up a trail of dark smoke below scattered white clouds, and a long flat-topped mesa runs across the horizon above a plain of low scrub, fences and telegraph poles.
feed.lookAt: Standing above the train roofs, the two rails and the row of poles converge on a coaling tower, and the mesa runs across the back. A vantage on top of a moving subject gives you the leading lines. Use a wide lens and keep the sky large, because the clouds add scale.

caption.title: Freight train near Laguna, New Mexico

feed.title: Baldy Hill, Craigieburn Range

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Craigieburn Range forms part of the Southern Alps in New Zealand's South Island. It lies on the south banks of the Waimakariri River, south of Arthur's Pass and west of State Highway 73, next to the Craigieburn Forest Park. Michal Klajban photographed Baldy Hill from Snowslide Valley on 9 June 2019 at about 15:45, in winter light. The picture shows a snow-covered summit lit by a low gold glow while a dark shadow cuts across the bare rock below it, and conifers fill the lower right corner under a grey sky.
feed.lookAt: A strip of low gold light touches the snowy summit while shadow swallows the slope beneath it, and the grey sky makes the lit peak glow. Look for the moment when cloud gaps spotlight one feature, and expose for the bright snow so the shadows stay deep.

feed.title: Constanța Casino at blue hour

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Art Nouveau, designed by Daniel Renard

feed.story: The Constanța Casino stands on the Black Sea seafront in the historic Peninsulă District of Constanța, Romania. Three buildings were constructed in the district to house a casino, the first a wooden structure in 1880. The current building is in Art Nouveau style, designed and built to the plans of Daniel Renard and inaugurated in August 1910. It is considered a symbol of the city and is listed as a historic monument. Diego Delso made this HDR view on 27 May 2016 at about 20:25, at blue hour, with the facade lit against a deep blue sky.
feed.lookAt: The lit facade glows warm against a deep blue sky at blue hour, and the sea behind it is almost black. Arrive in the twenty minutes after sunset, when sky and building lights balance, and use a tripod and a low ISO to keep the carved detail clean.

feed.title: Belt Railway clearing yard, Chicago

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano (1914–1997) worked for the Farm Security Administration after emigrating from the Russian Empire, and he later spent much of his life in Puerto Rico. The Library of Congress gives this colour transparency, dated January 1943, the title Belt Railway, looking toward the west yard of the clearing yard, taken from the bridge of the hump, Chicago, Illinois. Snow lies over a wide yard of crossing tracks, with white steam rising at the upper left and a floodlight tower on the right. A single worker stands at the lower right beside a boxcar, and long shadows from the poles lie across the snow.
feed.lookAt: Snow-covered tracks cross in curves below a high bridge, steam billows at the upper left, and one small worker at the lower right gives the whole yard its scale. Shoot from above to turn infrastructure into a pattern. Wait for steam and a person to enter the frame together.

feed.title: Nigeen Lake, Srinagar

image.credit: KennyOMG (edit by UnpetitproleX), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Nigeen Lake, also spelled Nageen Lake
Linked to Dal Lake by a narrow strait

feed.story: Nigeen Lake, also spelled Nageen Lake, lies in Srinagar, Jammu and Kashmir, India. It is sometimes considered a part of Dal Lake and is connected to it by a narrow strait. It is also joined to the Khushal Sar and Gil Sar lakes by a channel known as Nallah Amir Khan. The article calls it mildly eutrophic, meaning rich in nutrients. This panorama, taken on 19 April 2010 and later edited, shows the west bank with the distant Pir Panjal mountain range behind it. A long band of houses and trees sits on the shoreline and doubles in the still water.
feed.lookAt: The panorama is a thin horizontal band, with trees and houses mirrored in flat water and mountains faint behind them. A wide strip suits a long, quiet subject. Wait for calm air so the reflection stays crisp, and leave the sky and water almost empty.

feed.title: Palau de les Arts, Valencia

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Palau de les Arts Reina Sofía is an opera house, performing arts centre and urban landmark designed by Santiago Calatrava to anchor the northwest end of the City of Arts and Sciences in Valencia, Spain. It opened on 8 October 2005, and its first opera staging was Beethoven's Fidelio on 25 October 2006. Diliff made this image in January 2007 as a 3×5 segment panorama with a Canon 5D and a 24–105mm f/4L IS lens, according to the Commons description. The white shell arches over the glass frontage at night, and its shape repeats in the still water of the pool below.
feed.lookAt: At night the white shell curves over the lit glass front, and its shape repeats in the still pool below. Look for symmetry between a building and its reflection. Shoot from a low, wide position beside the water and wait for the surface to settle.

caption.title: Palau de les Arts, Valencia
caption.line2: Diliff · City of Arts and Sciences

feed.title: Jefferson General Store, Texas

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith (born 1946) is an American photographer whose work documents the landscapes, architecture and people of the United States in a nationwide study in progress since the 1980s. She has donated her photographs to the Library of Congress since 1992, and all of them are in the public domain. This one was taken on 20 May 2014 and is titled a 1950s-vintage truck outside a general store in Jefferson, a town in Marion County in East Texas on whose main street almost every commercial building has a historic marker. A pale blue pickup sits at the kerb in front of a two-storey brick store with red, white and blue bunting.
feed.lookAt: A pale blue truck sits at the kerb in front of a two-storey brick store, and its colour matches the sky above the building. Match one object to the sky to tie a frame together. Shoot square to the facade, and use the bunting's repeating curves as a line that runs across the bottom.

caption.title: Jefferson General Store, Texas
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Padum road below the Zanskar Range

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Zanskar Range, Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh

feed.story: The Zanskar Range is a mountain range in northern India, spanning Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh, that separates the Zanskar valley from the Indus valley. It lies parallel to the Great Himalayas and the Ladakh Range, and is geologically part of the Tethys Himalaya. Timothy A. Gonsalves took this picture on 6 June 2024 at about 09:45 on the Padum–Pibiting road from Karsha to Padum. The file description says the range towers 2,400 m above Padum, which sits at 3,500 m. A narrow road runs straight toward snowy peaks and a single tiny vehicle can be seen far ahead.
feed.lookAt: A straight road runs to the middle of the frame and ends below white peaks, with a speck of a vehicle far ahead for scale. Roads make strong leading lines in big landscapes. Stand on the centre line, use a lens that keeps the peaks large, and wait for a vehicle.

caption.title: Padum road below the Zanskar Range

feed.title: Correios Building, São Paulo

image.credit: Wilfredor, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Correios Building stands in República, one of 96 districts of the city of São Paulo, Brazil. The Wikipedia article for the district reports a population of 60,720 in the 2022 census. Wilfredor photographed the building on 12 October 2016 at about 14:13, and the file is titled simply Correios Building, São Paulo, Brazil. In the frame, a pale classical facade with a clock tower on its roof is lit from below against a deep blue sky, with warm light in its tall windows and a cobbled square in the foreground.
feed.lookAt: The facade glows warm from lights below while the sky stays a deep, saturated blue. A clock face on the roof adds a point of interest. Shoot just after dusk so the sky still holds colour, and keep the camera level so the vertical lines stay straight.

feed.title: Cotton hoers near Clarksdale, Mississippi

image.credit: Dorothea Lange, New York Public Library, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Dorothea Lange (1895–1965) was an American documentary photographer, best known for her Depression-era work for the Farm Security Administration. Her photographs, the article says, humanized the consequences of the Great Depression. This one comes from the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture at the New York Public Library, with the caption: these cotton hoers work from 6 a.m. to 7 p.m. for $1.00 near Clarksdale, Mississippi, June–July 1937. Lange stands behind a line of workers walking along a field path with hoes over their shoulders, their backs to the camera, and the figures grow smaller toward the distance.
feed.lookAt: The camera follows the workers from behind, and a line of hoes over their shoulders makes a rhythm that leads away along the path. Shooting from behind lets the viewer walk with the subjects. Use a low angle, and wait for the strides to line up.

caption.title: Cotton hoers near Clarksdale, Mississippi
caption.line2: Dorothea Lange · New York Public Library

feed.title: Khrang Suri waterfall, Meghalaya

image.credit: Chirnzb (edit by UnpetitproleX), CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Khrang Suri waterfall lies in the West Jaintia Hills district of Meghalaya, India, and the nearest town is Jowai. Meghalaya, whose name means "the abode of clouds", became a state on 21 January 1972, and the article says it is the wettest region of India. The picture was taken from the hilltop on 12 February 2017, as the file description records. Two thin falls drop over a rock ledge into a bright turquoise pool, with a dense green forest on both sides and a pale river bending away at the top of the frame.
feed.lookAt: Seen from above, two pale ribbons of water fall into a turquoise pool that stands out against the dark green forest. Climb to a high viewpoint to flatten the scene into shapes and colour. Let the pool sit low in the frame and use the river's bend to lead the eye upward.

feed.title: El Atazar Dam, Madrid

image.credit: Carlos Delgado, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Arch dam on the Lozoya River

feed.story: El Atazar Dam is an arch dam built near Madrid, Spain, on the Lozoya River, very close to where the Lozoya joins the Jarama. The curved design is optimum for the narrow gorge in which it was built, and arch dams are thin and need less material than other dam types. Construction started in 1968 and finished in 1972. The dam is 134 m high and was built to store and regulate water only, not to provide energy. Carlos Delgado photographed it on 2 May 2014 at about 14:09 from a high viewpoint above the road, with the reservoir stretching behind it.
feed.lookAt: From high on the hillside, the curved wall, the road and the gorge all fit in one view, with the reservoir stretching to blue hills. A high vantage turns a structure into a diagram of how it works. Include the road for scale, and keep the horizon in the top third.

feed.title: Roots, Foster Garden, Hawaii

image.credit: Ansel Adams, Honolulu Museum of Art, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams (1902–1984) was an American landscape photographer and environmentalist known for his black-and-white images of the American West. He helped found Group f/64, whose members advocated pure photography with sharp focus and the full tonal range of a print. This picture is Roots, Foster Garden, Hawaii, made in 1948. The Commons description identifies it as a gelatin silver print held by the Honolulu Museum of Art, accession 20558. Thick buttress roots spread across the ground like ribbons, curving through the frame with small round leaves scattered between them, and the print is signed at the lower right.
feed.lookAt: Thick roots curve across the frame like ribbons, and small round leaves scatter between them. There is no horizon, so the picture is all line and tone. Look straight down, fill the frame with the pattern, and use side light so the ridges of the roots carry the shape.

caption.title: Roots, Foster Garden, Hawaii
caption.line2: Ansel Adams · Honolulu Museum of Art

feed.title: Everest and the Khumbu Icefall from the west

image.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: West face of Lhotse-Nuptse massif, Khumbu Glacier
Khumbu Icefall, on Everest's western spur

feed.story: Mount Everest is the highest mountain in the world. This picture, taken by Vyacheslav Argenberg on 19 October 2009 at about 15:27, shows Everest, the Everest West Shoulder, the west face of the Lhotse-Nuptse massif, the Khumbu Glacier and the Khumbu Icefall, seen from the west in late afternoon sun, according to the Commons description. The icefall later became known for the ice avalanche of 18 April 2014, when seracs on the western spur of Everest failed and killed sixteen climbing Sherpas. In the frame, snow and ice fill the middle ground under a deep blue sky, and the dark summit sits beyond them.
feed.lookAt: Late sun picks out the ridges of snow and leaves the rock faces dark, and the very blue sky makes the white shapes stand out. Shoot with the sun to the side to get texture. Underexpose slightly to protect the snow, and let the dark summit anchor the pale foreground.

caption.title: Everest and the Khumbu Icefall from the west

feed.title: Monks at Preah Pithu, Angkor

image.credit: JJ Harrison (https://www.jjharrison.com.au/), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Preah Pithu, a group of five temples at Angkor

feed.story: Preah Pithu is a group of five temples at Angkor, Cambodia. The Wikipedia article says they were in all probability not designed as a group, and that despite their ruined state the remains have good decorative carving and a semi-wooded setting that is attractive and peaceful. JJ Harrison photographed a group of monks at Preah Pithu U on 27 April 2013 at about 07:45, according to the Commons description. In the picture, four monks in bright orange robes stand and sit in a doorway of grey moss-covered stone, with carved panels around them.
feed.lookAt: Four orange robes stand out against grey, moss-streaked stone, and the doorway frames them. When a person's colour is the opposite of the setting, a small figure carries the whole picture. Wait until each person has a different pose, then press the shutter.

feed.title: Cathedral Cove, Coromandel

image.credit: Krzysztof Golik, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Te Whanganui-o-Hei, or Cathedral Cove, Marine Reserve lies in the southern part of Mercury Bay on the Coromandel Peninsula in New Zealand and covers 840 hectares. Part of it lies off the Cathedral Cove Recreation Reserve, and with attractions such as a natural rock archway and neighbouring beaches, the area receives around 150,000 visitors a year. Krzysztof Golik photographed the cove on 17 March 2019 at about 15:36. A small wave rolls onto pale sand, a handful of people stand near the arch, and green trees cling to the rock above the dark opening.
feed.lookAt: A small wave curls in the foreground, a few distant people give the arch its scale, and trees crown the pale cliff above the dark opening. Place the wave in the lower left to lead toward the arch. Time the shutter to when the white water is at its widest.

feed.title: Swissôtel The Stamford reflected, Singapore

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: 1986, then the tallest hotel in the world

feed.story: Swissôtel The Stamford, formerly The Westin Stamford, is a hotel in Singapore, designed by architect I. M. Pei. At 226 metres it was the tallest hotel in the world when it opened in 1986, and it remains one of Southeast Asia's tallest. It is part of the Raffles City complex and sits above City Hall MRT station and Esplanade MRT station. Basile Morin took this picture on 8 June 2018 at about 17:09 from the roof garden at level 6 of the National Gallery Singapore, where the tower is reflected in a basin of water set among low roofs, with other towers and a streaked evening sky behind.
feed.lookAt: The round tower stands tall in the centre while its reflection sits in a flat basin at the bottom, and low horizontal roofs divide the two. Look for water set into a building to find a second view of a landmark. Stand square to the tower and keep the verticals straight.

feed.title: Maroon Bells and Maroon Lake

image.credit: Rhododendrites, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Maroon Peak and North Maroon Peak

feed.story: The Maroon Bells are two peaks in the Elk Mountains, Maroon Peak and North Maroon Peak, separated by about 0.3 miles. They lie about 19 kilometres southwest of Aspen, Colorado, and both are fourteeners; Maroon Peak is 14,163 feet high. The Wikipedia article says the view of the Bells from the Maroon Creek valley is very heavily photographed. Rhododendrites shot this version on 1 August 2017 at about 12:24, with Maroon Lake in the foreground. A meadow of wildflowers fills the bottom of the frame, dark forest climbs both sides, and snow still lies in the gullies of the peaks.
feed.lookAt: A meadow of flowers anchors the bottom, a pale lake sits at the left, and the peaks rise in the distance with snow in their gullies. On a heavily photographed subject, look for what is yours: a low angle on the flowers, or a tighter crop of the bells and their snow.

feed.title: Dvarapala bas-relief, Banteay Kdei

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Banteay Kdei, a Buddhist temple at Angkor
Mid-12th to early 13th century, under Jayavarman VII

feed.story: Banteay Kdei is a Buddhist temple in Angkor, Cambodia, built in the mid-12th to early 13th centuries during the reign of Jayavarman VII. It is in the Bayon architectural style, similar in plan to Ta Prohm and Preah Khan but less complex and smaller. The article says its structures are contained within two successive enclosure walls. The complex is dilapidated because of faulty construction and the poor quality of its sandstone, and renovation is under way. Diego Delso photographed this bas-relief of a dvarapala, a guardian figure, on 16 August 2013 at about 14:34. The figure stands in a recess holding a sword, with green lichen around it.
feed.lookAt: A calm guardian figure stands in a carved recess, and green lichen frames the weathered stone around him. Soft, even light brings out the carving without harsh shadows. Take a straight-on view with a vertical crop, and fill the frame so the figure's surface texture is the subject.

feed.title: Monument Valley from Forrest Gump Point

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Up to 1,000 ft (300 m) above the valley floor
Tsé Biiʼ Ndzisgaii, "valley of the rocks"

feed.story: Monument Valley is a region of the Colorado Plateau characterized by a cluster of sandstone buttes, the largest reaching 1,000 feet above the valley floor. Its Navajo name, Tsé Biiʼ Ndzisgaii, means "valley of the rocks", and the valley is considered sacred by the Navajo Nation. The article notes that director John Ford used it for several Westerns. King of Hearts photographed this view from Forrest Gump Point on U.S. Route 163 on 21 November 2018 at 06:55, shortly after dawn. The road runs straight toward distant buttes, with a pink and lilac sky above and red rock on both sides.
feed.lookAt: At dawn the sky turns pink and lilac while the buttes stay a flat violet silhouette at the end of a straight road. The centre line is a strong leading line. Arrive before sunrise, use a longer lens to stack the buttes, and keep the road's yellow dashes in the lower third.

caption.title: Monument Valley from Forrest Gump Point

feed.title: Prague astronomical clock dial

image.credit: Godot13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Mikuláš of Kadaň and Jan Šindel

feed.story: The Prague astronomical clock, or Prague Orloj, is a medieval astronomical clock attached to the Old Town Hall in Prague. Its oldest part, the mechanical clock and astronomical dial, dates to 1410 and was created by the horologist Mikuláš of Kadaň and the Charles University professor Jan Šindel. The calendar dial and the Gothic sculptures were added around 1490. The dial shows the positions of the Sun and Moon, the zodiac and several kinds of time. Godot13 photographed the clock face on 28 July 2013 at about 09:56. The blue and gold dial fills the frame, with carved figures standing on both sides of it.
feed.lookAt: The round dial fills the frame, with a ring of gold numerals, a gold sun pointer at the centre, and carved figures standing at both sides. A tight crop turns a landmark into a pattern. Photograph it straight on from a distance with a longer lens, so the circle stays round and the lines stay square.

feed.title: Cu Đê River

image.credit: Christopher Crouzet, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Cu Đê River, also called the Trường Định River, is a river of Da Nang, Vietnam. This view shows it just before it merges with Da Nang Bay, with fishing nets hanging over the water. Christopher Crouzet made the photograph on 22 March 2015 at 17:57, in the last hours of daylight, when the sky over the hills on the far shore turns to soft pink and the water repeats it. The frame is an extreme panorama, much wider than it is tall, so the calm river and the low ridge of hills can run across it without interruption.
feed.lookAt: Crop wide when the subject is a horizon. Here the water takes the lower half and the pink sky the upper, and the nets hanging at left and right act as counterweights. Soft pink in the water ties the foreground to the sky.

feed.title: Stongdey

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Stongdey, also spelled Stongde, Stongday, Tongde, Tongdey or Tangday, is a small village in the Zanskar valley of Ladakh, India. It sits on the right bank of the Zanskar River about 18 km northeast of Padum, on the Padum–Nimmu highway. The article on it also covers the neighbouring village of Kumik (Khumi). Timothy A. Gonsalves photographed it from the northeast on 7 June 2024 at 10:11, with the snow-capped Zanskar Range as the backdrop. A small white structure stands in the foreground, with green fields and the village below the ridge.
feed.lookAt: Scale is the lesson. The village is a few small roofs and a green patch, yet the range behind it fills most of the frame, and that contrast tells you how big the valley is. The small white structure in the foreground gives a second reference point. Keep a human-sized object in a mountain frame.

feed.title: Service Wings, New Orleans

image.credit: Arnold Genthe, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arnold Genthe was a German-American photographer, best known for his photographs of Northern California, San Francisco's Chinatown and the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, and for portraits of politicians, socialites and entertainers. This picture, titled Service Wings (Slave Quarters), New Orleans, shows Architect Row, row houses built in 1832 along Architect Street, as they looked between 1920 and 1926. The Library of Congress notes that the back portions of such houses were originally quarters for household slaves, and by the early twentieth century were often cheap apartments. The neighbourhood is run down, and two goats roam the open ground in the foreground.
feed.lookAt: Genthe stood far enough back to show the whole row, with balconies and brick chimneys on the horizon. The two goats in the foreground are small but decisive: they place the scene in time and say something about neglect. A flat, grey light keeps every texture visible.

feed.title: Shinku La

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Shinku La, also called Shingo La, is a mountain pass on the Nimmu–Padum–Darcha road, on the state boundary between Ladakh and Himachal Pradesh. It connects the Zanskar region of Ladakh with the Lahaul region of Himachal Pradesh. A Shingo La Tunnel is under construction, with a target completion date of 2028; it is expected to cut the Manali to Kargil distance by 522 km. Timothy A. Gonsalves photographed the road winding up to the pass on 4 October 2022 at 10:05. His note gives the elevation as 4,975 m and the peaks as about 5,600 m.
feed.lookAt: A road is a ready-made leading line. Here it zigzags across the slope and carries the eye from the lower left up toward the pass, while the snowy peaks and a hard blue sky fill the top. Look for a path that folds back on itself; each switchback adds depth.

caption.title: Shinku La
caption.line2: Timothy A. Gonsalves · Lahaul, Himachal Pradesh

feed.title: Spiti River

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Spiti is a high-altitude region of the Himalayas in the north-east of Himachal Pradesh, India. Its name means the middle land, the land between Tibet and India. It has a cold desert environment and is among the least populated regions of India. Timothy A. Gonsalves photographed the Spiti River above Kaza on 20 June 2018 at 15:29, at an elevation of 3,600 m. His note says the river bed is several hundred metres wide, while the river itself is much narrower and meanders along it, braided into pale threads across the gravel.
feed.lookAt: The river is the smallest thing here and still the main subject. Pale braided channels cut through a wide, dull gravel bed and lead you back toward the mountains. When you shoot from high above, look for a line of water that carries the eye through the frame.

caption.title: Spiti River
caption.line2: Timothy A. Gonsalves · Spiti, Himachal Pradesh

feed.title: 17-Mile Drive, Monterey

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith is an American photographer whose work documents the landscapes, architecture and people of the United States. She has donated her photographs to the Library of Congress since 1992, a collection of nearly 100,000 images, all in the public domain. She began her nationwide project after photographing the Willard Hotel in the early 1980s for its restoration. This picture, titled 17-Mile Drive, scenic road through Monterey, California, has its title, date and keywords provided by the photographer; the file's Exif data records 10 June 2012. It belongs to the Jon B. Lovelace Collection of California Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America Project.
feed.lookAt: A breaking wave is a matter of timing. The photographer caught the spray just as it burst against the dark rocks, so the white shape holds its form against the blue. Use a fast shutter, pick a rock for the wave to hit, and wait for the next set.

caption.title: 17-Mile Drive, Monterey
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Kimono Forest

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Kimono Forest is a decoration project at Arashiyama Station, the western terminus of the Randen Arashiyama Line in Kyoto, Japan. It is a collection of nearly 600 kimono gowns wrapped around poles with LED lighting inside, developed by the designer Yasumichi Morita. The textile is dyed in the Kyo-yuzen style, covered and sealed with acrylic fibre and shaped into cylindrical poles about 2 metres tall, installed around the station and the railway tracks. Basile Morin photographed it at night on 10 June 2019, with the stone-paved walkway running between the glowing poles.
feed.lookAt: Repetition makes pattern. The poles shrink toward a vanishing point at the end of the paved path, and each one is lit from inside, so the colour comes from the subject, not the sky. Stand centred, level the camera, and let the symmetry do the work.

feed.title: Chah

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Chah, also called Cha, is a small village and one of the tehsils in the Lungnak valley of Zanskar district, Ladakh, India. It lies at the base of a mountain range on the right bank of the Tsarap River, on the Padum–Darcha road, 47 km south of Padum. Timothy A. Gonsalves photographed the village from that road on 5 June 2024 at 11:16. His caption describes newly sown fields with a mountain backdrop, and the small patches of field below the village are visible as pale and green terraces against the bare slope.
feed.lookAt: Texture can be the subject. The pale and green field patches make a patchwork against the bare grey slope, and the village shrinks to a few white dots on the ridge. Put the horizon high, give the foreground its space, and let the land fill most of the frame.

feed.title: 15 Belgo Road, Lakeville

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith is an American photographer who has documented the landscapes, architecture and people of the United States in a nationwide study in progress since the 1980s. Her work is donated to the Library of Congress and is in the public domain. This picture is titled 15 Belgo Road, Lakeville, Connecticut. The Library's notes say the building was designed by architect Alfredo De Vito and built in 1985, and that the photographer provided the title and date; the file's Exif data records 11 October 2011. It is part of the George F. Landegger Collection of Connecticut Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America.
feed.lookAt: The low vantage turns a house into a monument. Standing at the foot of the lawn, the photographer lets the white volumes rise against a sky full of streaked cloud, and the grass becomes a large green foreground. A vertical frame suits the height; autumn trees add warm contrast.

caption.title: 15 Belgo Road, Lakeville
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Trunkol Meadow

image.credit: UnpetitproleX, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kashmir is the northernmost geographical region of the Indian subcontinent. Until the mid-19th century the name meant only the Kashmir Valley, between the Great Himalayas and the Pir Panjal Range. In the first millennium the region became an important centre of Buddhism. This photograph, taken on 10 August 2024 at 15:16, shows horses grazing at Trunkol meadow on the way to Gangabal lake in the Indian territory of Jammu and Kashmir. A chestnut horse grazes in the foreground, a second stands further up the slope, and forested ridges fade into the haze behind.
feed.lookAt: Two animals, two distances. The chestnut horse is in the foreground and the white-and-brown one higher on the slope sits in the same frame, so the eye moves between them and then out to the layered ridges behind. Wait for the head to lower or the leg to move.

feed.title: Shivaliks and the Middle Himalayas

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Himachal Pradesh, whose name means the Snow-laden Mountain Province, is a state in the north of India in the Western Himalayas. This aerial view looks east from near Shimla across the Shivaliks and the Middle Himalayas. Timothy A. Gonsalves took it on 16 February 2020 at 10:30 and notes that some haze reduction gives a Roerich-like scene. Ridge after ridge stacks up in progressively paler blue, and a long band of snow-capped peaks closes the horizon, beneath a thin layer of cloud that fills the upper part of the sky.
feed.lookAt: Haze is a depth tool. Each ridge is paler than the one in front, so distance reads as colour, not detail. Shoot from height, let the layers stack, and keep the snow line as the final steady band at the top.

feed.title: Gullfoss

image.credit: Pierre-Selim Huard, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Gullfoss, meaning Golden Falls, is a waterfall in the canyon of the Hvítá river in southwest Iceland, between the municipalities of Bláskógabyggð and Hrunamannahreppur. It is one of the most popular tourist attractions in the country and is included in Golden Circle tours of the countryside near Reykjavík. Pierre-Selim Huard photographed it under snow on 22 February 2017 at 16:27. Snow covers both rims of the gorge and the ledges below, while the water is a deep blue-green where it leaves the pool and a pale mist rises out of the canyon.
feed.lookAt: Winter strips colour out and leaves shape. The falls are the only moving, saturated thing in a white and grey frame, so the teal water pulls the eye at once. Overcast light keeps the snow from clipping; expose to keep its texture.

feed.title: Lake Clearwater

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Lake Clearwater, in Māori Te Puna-a-Taka, is a high country lake in the Ashburton District of the South Island of New Zealand. It has a surface area of 197 hectares and sits at 667 metres. The lake lies among rugged mountain country, tussocklands, beech forest and wetlands between the Rakaia and Rangitata Rivers, and is a protected wildlife refuge managed by the Department of Conservation. Michal Klajban photographed it on 22 September 2019 at 06:35, with snowy Mt Potts (2,184 m) behind. Bare shrubs frame the foreground and the still water repeats the peaks.
feed.lookAt: Be early. At 06:35 the peaks catch the first warm light while the lake stays in cool shadow and holds a clean reflection. Bare branches in the foreground make a natural frame; place them at both sides and let the mountain sit between them.

feed.title: Digermulen

image.credit: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Digermulen is a village in Vågan Municipality, Nordland county, Norway, on the southwestern tip of the large island of Hinnøya. There is a ferry connection to the nearby island of Stormolla. This photograph, taken on 21 September 2015, shows a small white boat at Digermulen port, afloat on the water. The mountains Litlkorsnestinden and Korsnestinden in the background are on the island of Austvågøya. The water is so still that the peaks are mirrored almost exactly, and a strip of yellow autumn trees on the near shore separates the real mountain from its reflection.
feed.lookAt: A mirror gives you two pictures in one. The reflection repeats the ridge, so the centre of the frame is the shoreline where they meet. The small boat in the lower left supplies scale and a point of interest. Shoot when the wind drops.

feed.title: Kathleen Lake

image.credit: Jakub Fryš, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kathleen Lake is in Yukon, Canada, south of Haines Junction within Kluane National Park and Reserve. It is the largest lake wholly within the park, with an area of 3,376 hectares and a maximum depth of 111 metres. The water is exceptionally clear, and kokanee salmon live and reproduce in it. The lake was named for a girl from Berwickshire, Scotland, left behind by William Scotty Hume, a North-West Mounted Police constable stationed on the Dalton Trail from 1900 to 1902. Jakub Fryš photographed it in the evening, at 22:25 on 25 May.
feed.lookAt: The photograph catches a wave just as it breaks. The white crest repeats the snow on the mountain, and the stones at lower left lead to a driftwood stump. Use a fast shutter to freeze foam, and shoot in the low evening light that warms the peaks.

feed.title: Huacachina

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Huacachina is a village built in a small oasis about five kilometres from the city of Ica in southwestern Peru. It has a permanent population of around 100 people, although many tourists visit each year, and the oasis was featured on the back of the 50 nuevo sol note in 1991. The name comes from Quechua, wakachina, meaning guard or conceal, possibly shortened from wakachina qucha, hidden lagoon. Diego Delso photographed it on 29 July 2015. A green lagoon and a cluster of palms sit in a bowl of pale dunes, with small figures walking the ridge.
feed.lookAt: Contrast of colour and scale. A small patch of green water and trees sits inside a huge, uniform bowl of sand, and that tells the story in one look. Notice the tiny figures on the dune; they give the dunes their size.

feed.title: L'Umbracle

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: L'Umbracle is part of the City of Arts and Sciences complex in Valencia, Spain, a sculpture garden and landscaped walk. Santiago Calatrava designed it as an entrance along the southwestern edge of the complex and as a cover over its car park, and it was completed in 2001. Its plantings use species native to Valencia, such as rockrose, lentisca, rosemary, honeysuckle, bougainvillea and palm trees. The photograph is an ultrawide panoramic view from inside, taken by Diliff in January 2007. White arches curve up from both sides and meet overhead above a straight walkway.
feed.lookAt: An ultrawide lens turns a repeating structure into a tunnel. Stand on the centre line of the walkway, so the arches curve evenly from both sides and meet overhead. Palms break the rigid geometry, and the two walkers give the whole scale.

feed.title: Portas da Cidade

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ponta Delgada, meaning Thin Cape, is the largest municipality and the executive capital of the Autonomous Region of the Azores in Portugal. It is on São Miguel, the largest and most populous island of the archipelago, and had 67,287 inhabitants in 2021. The Portas da Cidade, the City Gates, are shown here in a photograph made by Diego Delso on 29 July 2020, combined from several frames in HDR. The three arches glow violet under artificial lighting against a deep blue evening sky, with street lamps and a monument standing in the square beyond.
feed.lookAt: Shoot in blue hour, not at night. The sky still has depth and colour, and the lamps and coloured floodlights are balanced against it. Placing the camera on the central axis makes the arches symmetrical and frames the monument beyond them.

feed.title: Jamnik

image.credit: Mihael Grmek, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jamnik is a settlement on the eastern slopes of the Jelovica Plateau in the Municipality of Kranj, in the Upper Carniola region of Slovenia. The photograph looks toward the Church of Saints Primus and Felician, which stands on a small green hill. Mihael Grmek took it on 30 August 2015 at 09:29, in morning light. The slope is mowed meadow dotted with trees; beyond the church the land drops away, and several layers of blue mountains rise in the haze. The frame is a wide panorama, so the whole scene is held at once.
feed.lookAt: The tiny church is the whole composition. It sits off-centre on the crest of the hill, small against ridge after ridge, and the diagonal of the meadow slopes toward it. In morning haze, the distant peaks fade, which makes the nearer slope read as bright.

feed.title: Dragon Dune, Iquique

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Iquique is the capital of Iquique Province, a port city in the northern Chilean region of Tarapacá. This view shows the Dragon Dune in the foreground and the city behind it. The dune is about 20,000 years old and was formed by coastal winds when the sea level was 100 metres further inland. It is 6.4 kilometres long and 320 metres high, and it is stable, though it looks menacing from the bottom. It became a Natural Sanctuary in 2005, but earlier part of its west wing was removed to allow the city to grow. Diego Delso took the photograph on 11 February 2016.
feed.lookAt: The sand ridge acts like a giant diagonal. It starts in the lower right, a clean smooth line, and cuts the frame in two. On the left, a dense city meets a bright sea. Take a high vantage so the foreground and city sit in one frame.

feed.title: Étang de Thau

image.credit: Christian Ferrer, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Étang de Thau, or Bassin de Thau, is the largest of a string of lagoons that stretch along the French coast from the Rhône river to the foothills of the Pyrenees and the border with Spain. Although it has a high salinity, it is considered the third largest lake in France. Christian Ferrer photographed dawn over part of Sète and the lagoon on 17 May 2014 at 05:31. The sky is orange at the horizon and cool blue above, the water reflects it, and pink flowers on the slope fill the foreground in front of the town.
feed.lookAt: Dawn gives a gradient: warm at the horizon, cool above. Use flowers or a tree in the foreground as a frame, and keep them in shadow so the town stays the lighter, smaller shape beyond. Arrive before sunrise, because the best colour is short.

feed.title: Heimaey Harbour

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Heimaey is the largest and most populated island off the Icelandic coast, and the largest of the Vestmannaeyjar archipelago, at 13.4 square kilometres. It lies 4 nautical miles off the south coast of Iceland and had a population of 4,414 in 2022. In January 1973 lava flow from nearby Eldfell destroyed half the town and threatened to close its harbour, the town's main income source; an operation to cool the advancing lava with sea water saved the harbour. Diego Delso photographed the harbour in a panorama on 17 August 2014 at 10:31, with moored boats and green hills.
feed.lookAt: A panorama needs an anchor. Here the steep green headland sits at the right with red boats at its base, and calm water doubles the scene. Keep the horizon level and the camera steady between frames, and let the long, narrow crop emphasise the line of the harbour.

feed.title: Kåfjorden

image.credit: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kåfjorden, Gáivuotna in Northern Sami and Kaivuono in Kven, is a fjord in Gáivuotna Municipality (also known as Kåfjord Municipality) in Troms county, Norway. The fjord is 20 kilometres long and is a branch off the main Lyngen fjord, stretching further inland to the village of Birtavarre. The European route E06 highway runs around the entire fjord. Ximonic took this photograph in March 2012, looking west and northwest from the northeast coast. A red boat and a small wooden shed sit on the snowy shore, with snow-covered mountains across the blue water.
feed.lookAt: Snow and a low sun make colour pop. The red boat is the only warm spot in a blue and white scene, so the eye goes straight to it. Place it away from the centre, leave room for the mountains, and watch the exposure so the snow keeps its texture.

feed.title: Salar de Ascotán

image.credit: Kabelleger / David Gubler, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Runs over 35 km along the west side

feed.story: Salar de Ascotán, also known as Salar de Cebollar, is a salt flat in northern Chile. It has a surface area of 246 square kilometres, and its drainage basin of 1,455 square kilometres is shared with Bolivia. The salt pan was once filled by a lake of about 270 square kilometres. Today the FCAB railway runs along the west side of the flat for more than 35 kilometres. David Gubler photographed three FCAB locomotives pulling a train of ore buckets across it in April 2012, on the journey from Calama to Ollagüe at the Bolivian border. The 5,846 metre stratovolcano Cerro del Azufre stands behind.
feed.lookAt: The train gives the empty salt flat a scale you can read at once. Its bright orange and yellow engines are the only strong colour against pale ground and a snow-capped volcano. Wait for a moving subject to enter an otherwise still landscape, and let its smoke point toward the mountain.

feed.title: Juntan Reservoir

image.credit: Zhangzhugang, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Juntan Reservoir, also known as Jiuxian Lake, is a vast reservoir in Guangfeng District of Shangrao, Jiangxi, China. It is one of the largest man-made lakes in Shangrao city. The article gives its surface area as 350 square kilometres and its storage capacity as some 52,700,000 cubic metres of water. Zhangzhugang photographed it on 4 September 2010. In this upright frame a tall rock outcrop topped with dense green forest rises from the shore, and a small boat sits on the dark green water below a sky of broken cloud.
feed.lookAt: A vertical frame suits a tall outcrop. The rock tower sits high in the picture while the curve of the shoreline leads the eye down to the small boat, which sets the scale. Look for a tiny human element that tells viewers how large the landscape really is.

feed.title: Edmund Pettus Bridge, Selma

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Edmund Pettus Bridge carries U.S. Route 80 Business over the Alabama River in Selma, Alabama. It is a steel through arch bridge, 1,248 feet long, built in 1939–1940 and opened on 25 May 1940. On 7 March 1965 police attacked civil rights marchers as they tried to cross it on their way to Montgomery. Carol M. Highsmith photographed people crossing the bridge on 7 March 2010, the 45th anniversary, to recreate that march. The bridge is named for Edmund Pettus, a Confederate brigadier general and U.S. senator. The Library of Congress says the title, date and subject note came from the photographer.
feed.lookAt: Standing on the roadway, the photographer lets the white arches repeat and shrink toward the far bank, with the bridge's name across the top. People walking make small figures that give the span its scale. Use repeating structure as a frame, and let a few people show what the place means.

caption.title: Edmund Pettus Bridge, Selma
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Dobson River

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

facts: Edward Dobson, by Julius von Haast

feed.story: The Dobson River (Māori: Ōtaao) is a river in the South Island of New Zealand. It flows south for 45 kilometres from its source on the west slope of Mount Edgar Thomson in the Southern Alps before joining the Hopkins River near Lake Ōhau. It was named by Julius von Haast in the 1860s for his father-in-law, Edward Dobson, the Canterbury Provincial Engineer. The Department of Conservation maintains a tramping track and several backcountry huts in the valley. Michal Klajban made this picture of Dobson Stream by Wharfedale hut on 14 June 2019, during the blue hour, with a tripod in the water.
feed.lookAt: A long exposure turns the stream into silk while the rocks stay sharp. The curve of the water leads upward to a pale moon in the dusk sky. Use a tripod, a small aperture and the blue hour, when sky and water are close in brightness, to keep detail in both.

feed.title: Golden Gate Canyon

image.credit: Acroterion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Golden Gate Canyon lies in the northwestern region of Yellowstone National Park in Wyoming. Glen Creek flows north through it, descending from 7,400 feet at Kingman Pass to just under 6,000 feet in less than three miles. A road was first built through the Golden Gate in 1884–85, directed by Lieutenant Dan Christie Kingman, who recorded the name that visitors gave the canyon for the yellow hue of its rocks. A wooden trestle was replaced by a concrete viaduct in 1900, and that was replaced in turn in 1930–34. Acroterion photographed it on 17 September 2010.
feed.lookAt: The road sweeps across the yellow cliff on its viaduct and gives the frame a strong diagonal. Dark conifers on the right balance the pale rock on the left, and clouds fill the open sky. When a man-made line crosses a landscape, use it to lead the eye through the picture.

feed.title: Boutique, Marché aux Halles, Paris

image.credit: Eugène Atget, Metropolitan Museum of Art, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Eugène Atget (1857–1927) photographed Paris, and this gelatin silver print shows a shop at the Marché aux Halles. The Metropolitan Museum of Art dates the picture to 1925 and notes that it was printed around 1929, two years after Atget died. Berenice Abbott, the American photographer, is also listed as an artist on the file, which suggests her connection to the later print. The print measures 23.1 by 17 centimetres, and the Met released it into the public domain under CC0. The file page gives no further description of the shop.
feed.lookAt: A dark shop opening becomes a frame inside the frame. A single bulb and a cluster of small objects sit in the middle of the black space, while the pale border of the print sets it off. Look for doorways and windows that isolate a small scene, and let shadow do the framing.

caption.title: Boutique, Marché aux Halles, Paris
caption.line2: Eugène Atget · Metropolitan Museum of Art

feed.title: Quinault Rain Forest

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Quinault Rain Forest is a temperate rain forest in Olympic National Park and the Olympic National Forest in Washington. It lies in the valley formed by the Quinault River and Lake Quinault, called the Valley of the Rain Forest Giants because of the record-size trees found there, including Western Red Cedar, Sitka Spruce and Douglas fir. The forest receives an average of 17 feet of rain a year. King of Hearts photographed Merriman Falls here on 10 June 2018, where a thin stream drops down mossy boulders beneath tall trunks.
feed.lookAt: Green dominates this frame, from moss on the boulders to ferns and the canopy. Soft, overcast light keeps contrast low, which lets the white thread of the falls stand out. Look for water that cascades in steps, and use a slow shutter to blur it while the moss stays crisp.

caption.title: Quinault Rain Forest
caption.line2: King of Hearts · Olympic National Park, Washington

feed.title: Cirque de Gavarnie

image.credit: Benh Lieu Song, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Cirque de Gavarnie is a vast cirque in the central Pyrenees, in southwestern France near the Spanish border. Its rock walls rise up to 1,500 metres above the floor, which is 800 metres wide at the deepest point and about 3,000 metres wide at the top. Victor Hugo described it as the Colosseum of nature. Gavarnie Falls, the second-highest waterfall in Europe, drops 422 metres. The cirque was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1997. Benh Lieu Song photographed the valley on 22 June 2009 from a high vantage point.
feed.lookAt: From a high viewpoint the valley floor becomes a green foreground that leads toward the wall of rock. Layers of ridge fade from dark to pale, and patches of snow mark the distance. Include a sweep of foreground to give a mountain scene depth and a sense of the journey.

feed.title: A boat on a river in China

image.credit: Arthur Rothstein, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arthur Rothstein (1915–1985) was an American photographer whose career spanned five decades and who was recognised as one of America's premier photojournalists. This 1946 photograph from the Library of Congress shows a boat on a river with rolling hills behind. The description places it in Kiangsu Province or Yunnan Province in China, so the exact place is uncertain. The Library of Congress holds the original under digital ID ppmsca.07797, and a restored version also exists on Commons. Wikimedia Commons categorises it as 1946 in China and Junks of China. The library knows of no copyright restrictions on it.
feed.lookAt: The junk sits on still water with its sails and reflection joined. Dark hills close the frame above a low horizon, and the pale sky stays plain. Wait for calm water to double a subject, and keep the horizon low so reflection and subject have room.

caption.title: A boat on a river in China

feed.title: Mount Rainier

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Mount Rainier, also known as Tahoma, is a large, active stratovolcano in the Cascade Range of the Pacific Northwest. It stands in Mount Rainier National Park about 59 miles south-southeast of Seattle. At 14,406 feet it is the highest mountain in Washington and the most topographically prominent in the contiguous United States. Because of its glacial ice and proximity to a major urban area, it is considered one of the most dangerous volcanoes in the world. Timothy A. Gonsalves photographed it from the west on 11 March 2023, from a flight between Seattle and Los Angeles.
feed.lookAt: The snowy summit rises out of a flat layer of cloud like an island. Shooting from a plane window gives you this view for only moments, so keep the camera ready and the settings set. Expose for the bright snow, and let the blue sky above and the cloud below frame the peak.

feed.title: Hullathy

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Hullathy is a Gram Panchayat and village in the Nilgiris district of Tamil Nadu, India. The panchayat is responsible for 32 villages with a population of 9,187, covering 2,729 hectares along both sides of a road that descends steeply down the Sigur Ghat from Ooty to Masinagudi. Timothy A. Gonsalves photographed the western villages on 29 November 2024, looking southwest from below Melur. His description calls it a steep valley in the north face of the Nilgiri Mountains, in the rain shadow, where villagers grow vegetables and tea on terraces with irrigation.
feed.lookAt: Terraces, small villages and two hills with cloud on the summits make layered planes in this frame. The light stripes of fields lead the eye across the slope. From a high viewpoint, look for patterns in farmland, and let a hill with cloud on top close the picture.

caption.title: Hullathy
caption.line2: Timothy A. Gonsalves · Nilgiris district, Tamil Nadu

feed.title: A Chicago and North Western railroad roundhouse

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano (1914–1997) was a Ukrainian-born photographer who worked for the Farm Security Administration. This colour transparency, titled A Chicago and North Western railroad roundhouse, was made in December 1942 for the FSA and Office of War Information. The Library of Congress notes give the location as Proviso Yards, and the title comes from the agency caption. The transparency was transferred from the Office of War Information in 1944. Subject headings list railroad roundhouses, railroad shops and yards, and the Chicago and North Western Railway Company. Delano later spent much of his life in Puerto Rico, where he also worked as a composer and filmmaker.
feed.lookAt: A low curved roundhouse stretches across the width of the frame, with smoke from a chimney drifting in cold air. Snow and a clear winter sky give the picture a pale blue tone. Use a long, flat horizon and one plume of smoke to show a working place in winter light.

caption.title: A Chicago and North Western railroad roundhouse

feed.title: Raiwada Reservoir

image.credit: Saiphani02, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Sri Varada Narayana Murty Raiwada Reservoir, usually called Raiwada Reservoir, was built across the Sarada River near Raiwada village in Devarapalli mandal, Anakapalli district, 58 kilometres from Visakhapatnam. It is one of the main water sources for the city, with a capacity of 2,360 tcm, and the Irrigation and CAD Department maintains it. Saiphani02 photographed it on 11 August 2024. The description notes a tree on a small island, a duckling swimming, buffaloes grazing, boats standing by and cranes fishing, with a large mountain behind. Many small bodies of land can be seen over the waterbody.
feed.lookAt: A single tree on a small green island becomes the focus because everything else is low and flat. Its reflection doubles the shape in calm water, and the hill behind closes the frame. Look for one isolated subject in a wide scene and place it off centre.

feed.title: Lyngen

image.credit: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Lyngen, in Northern Sami Ivguvuotna, is a fjord in Troms county, Norway. At 82 kilometres it is the longest fjord in Troms and is often used as the dividing line between northern and southern Troms. The Lyngen Alps lie on the Lyngen Peninsula along its western shore, and the European route E06 runs along the eastern shore. Ximonic (Simo Räsänen) photographed a shed with a green roof on the east coast on 28 June 2012, in the late afternoon, with the mountains of the Lyngen Alps across the water. The fjord passes through five municipalities, including Skjervøy and Storfjord.
feed.lookAt: The turf-roofed shed anchors the foreground, and snow on the far mountains shows the distance across the fjord. Flowers in the long grass lead toward it. Get low, let a small human-made subject sit in the foreground, and use it to give a big landscape a story.

feed.title: Prasat Sikhoraphum

image.credit: JJ Harrison, CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Prasat Sikhoraphum is a Khmer temple in Thailand, located between the cities of Surin and Sisaket. It was built in the 12th century, and the article names King Suryavararas in connection with its builders. The temple was converted for use by Buddhists in the 16th century. Architectural contributions influenced by Laos are evident on the tower roofs. The name comes from the Sanskrit word shikhara, meaning tower sanctuary. JJ Harrison photographed it on 8 December 2012 from the central path, under a clear blue sky. The Exif data gives the time as 11:33 in the morning.
feed.lookAt: The path runs straight to the central tower and makes a symmetrical frame. Three brick towers on a low base repeat a rhythm, and green lawn and blue sky set off the warm stone. Stand on the axis of a symmetrical building and keep the camera level so the lines stay straight.

feed.title: Sari Temple

image.credit: Crisco 1492, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Sari Temple, also known as Candi Bendan, is an 8th-century Buddhist temple at Dusun Bendan, Tirtomartani village, Kalasan, Sleman Regency, Special Region of Yogyakarta, Indonesia. It lies about 130 metres northeast of the Kalasan temple. The temple was a two-story building with wooden beams, floors and stairs, with windows and doors, all of organic materials now decayed. It is suggested that it was a vihara, a dwelling place for monks. Crisco 1492 made this panorama on 10 April 2014 from 52 images. The name Sari, or Saré, translates as to sleep in Javanese, which fits its use as a dwelling.
feed.lookAt: A panorama stitched from many frames can keep a building's lines true while showing the whole of it. Here the stone temple stands against bright cloud, and the palm at left frames it. Shoot with overlap, keep the camera level, and rotate around the lens for clean joins.

feed.title: Nara Park

image.credit: Martin Falbisoner, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Nara Park is a public park in the city of Nara, Japan, at the foot of Mount Wakakusa. Established in 1880, it is one of the oldest parks in Japan and is designated a Place of Scenic Beauty. Over 1,200 wild sika deer roam freely in the park and are designated a natural treasure. The official size is about 502 hectares, and the area including the grounds of Tōdai-ji, Kōfuku-ji, Kasuga Grand Shrine and the Nara National Museum is about 660 hectares. Martin Falbisoner photographed this path on 15 November 2016.
feed.lookAt: Fallen red leaves cover the path and glow against the yellow maple overhead, so the whole picture is warm. Stone lanterns and a curved fence lead the eye along the bend. In autumn, shoot in soft light and use the path as a leading line.

feed.title: Don Khon

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Don Khon is an island in the Mekong River in the Si Phan Don archipelago, whose name means Four Thousand Islands, in Champasak Province of southern Laos. Basile Morin photographed it on 27 May 2018 in the late afternoon, from Don Det island. His description names the colourful floating bungalows of the Sala Don Khone Hotel on the Mekong bank, in front of tall palm trees. The wide, low frame follows the line of the bank, with palms rising behind the bungalows and a band of calm brown water in front.
feed.lookAt: A wide, low frame suits a long, horizontal bank. The bungalows' bright colours stand out against the palms, and the calm river reflects them. Use late afternoon light for warm colour, and look for repeating shapes that make a rhythm across a panorama.

feed.title: Kasbah Amridil

image.credit: Petar Milošević, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kasbah Amridil is a historic fortified residence, or kasbah, known as a tighremt in Amazigh, in the oasis of Skoura, in Morocco. It is considered among the most impressive kasbahs of its kind in Morocco and was formerly featured on the Moroccan 50 dirham note. Petar Milošević photographed it on 20 March 2024. He stands across a dry, stony riverbed, so the mud-brick walls and towers appear as a low band on the horizon beneath a clear blue sky. The file gives the time as 10:40 in the morning, and the description also gives the Arabic name قصبة امريديل.
feed.lookAt: The kasbah is small in the frame, yet it reads clearly because everything around it is bare ground and open sky. The rocky foreground gives scale to the distance. Leave plenty of empty space around a landmark to show how isolated and imposing it is.

feed.title: Bolungarvík

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Bolungarvík is a small town in the northwest of Iceland, on the Westfjords peninsula, about 14 kilometres from Ísafjörður and 473 kilometres from Reykjavík. It has been used as a fishing outpost since the 17th century. The village was not accessible by road until 1950, and a tunnel opened in 2010 to bypass the avalanche-prone old road. Tourist sites include the Ósvör Maritime Museum, a restored 19th-century fishing station. Diego Delso photographed it on 15 August 2014, with low cloud over the mountain and a boat beside the turf huts.
feed.lookAt: Low cloud hides the mountain top and softens the whole scene into grey and green. The turf huts and boat bring warm detail to the foreground. Overcast, misty weather can suit a place with a history of hard work, so shoot it as it is and keep the horizon calm.

feed.title: Regietów

image.credit: Pudelek, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Regietów is a village in the administrative district of Gmina Uście Gorlickie, within Gorlice County, Lesser Poland Voivodeship, in southern Poland, close to the border with Slovakia. Its name is written Регетів in Rusyn. Pudelek photographed a wooden bell tower at Regietów Wyżny on 15 July 2016. The small tower, with a shingled base and a cross on its roof, stands alone in a green meadow in front of a forested hill under heavy summer cloud. The photograph was taken at 18:40 in the evening, and the village name romanises from Rusyn as Rehetiv.
feed.lookAt: A single small structure stands alone in a green meadow, so the eye goes straight to it. The cross on top points toward dark clouds, and the forested hill closes the frame behind it. Place a lone building low in the picture and let sky and land fill the rest.

feed.title: Marina Bay

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Marina Bay is a bay in the Central Area of Singapore. The surrounding area, also called Marina Bay, is a 360 hectare extension to the adjacent Central Business District and the new downtown of Singapore, built on reclaimed land. Buildings include Gardens by the Bay, Marina Bay Sands and Marina Bay Financial Centre. The list continues with Asia Square, The Sail @ Marina Bay and Marina One. Basile Morin photographed the ArtScience Museum, designed by Moshe Safdie, on 5 June 2018 in the late afternoon, with the towers of the Central Business District behind it across the water.
feed.lookAt: The petal-shaped roof is the clear subject, and the skyline stays smaller behind it. Walkway and railing lines lead along the water toward it. Pick a vantage that separates a landmark from its background, and use soft, overcast light to keep the white forms clean.

feed.title: Catoctin Mountain

image.credit: Acroterion, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Catoctin Mountain, with the geologically associated Bull Run Mountains, forms the easternmost mountain ridge of the Blue Ridge Mountains, part of the Appalachian Mountains. The ridge runs northeast to southwest for about 50 miles, from South Mountain near Emmitsburg, Maryland, to the Piedmont near New Baltimore, Virginia. Acroterion photographed a farm in sunlight at the base of the mountain, between Thurmont and Emmitsburg, on 26 January 2023. There is snow on the higher mountain behind, and Camp David is on the summit. The ridge forms the eastern rampart of the Loudoun and Middletown valleys.
feed.lookAt: A patch of sun picks out the farm while the hill behind stays dark. That contrast makes the buildings glow. In winter, wait for a break in the cloud, expose for the lit area and let the shadows fall away, so one spot becomes the whole story.

feed.title: Reine

image.credit: Ximonic (Simo Räsänen), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Reine is the administrative centre of Moskenes Municipality in Nordland county, Norway. The fishing village is on the island of Moskenesøya in the Lofoten archipelago, above the Arctic Circle, about 300 kilometres southwest of Tromsø. Reine Church is located in the village, and the 0.28 square kilometre village had a population of 297 in 2023. The village has a population density of 1,061 inhabitants per square kilometre. Ximonic (Simo Räsänen) photographed an autumn view of the village at Reinefjorden on 27 September 2010, with rocky peaks rising behind the water and autumn colour in the shrubs of the foreground.
feed.lookAt: A wide panorama lets the village sit small between two sets of peaks. Autumn shrubs in the foreground add colour and depth, and the calm fjord mirrors the cloud. Use a foreground of seasonal colour to lead the eye into a distant landmark.

feed.title: Indus Valley near Leh

image.credit: KennyOMG, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Indus rises in the Tibet Autonomous Region, where it is called Sengge Zangbo, and runs 3,180 kilometres to the Arabian Sea near Karachi. It flows northwest through the Kashmir region, first through Ladakh and then Gilgit-Baltistan, before bending sharply after the Nanga Parbat massif and heading south through Pakistan. Its drainage basin covers about 1,120,000 square kilometres, and its glacier-fed flow makes it one of the fifty largest rivers on Earth. This panorama was made on 15 September 2009 from the Indus Viewpoint on the Srinagar–Leh Highway, near Leh, which stands on the river's bank at about 3,500 metres.
feed.lookAt: A panorama this wide lets one long diagonal do the work: the river braids through the tree-green valley floor and carries the eye from the dark foreground slope to the far snow peaks. Brown ridges on both sides frame it. Wait for clouds, as here, so the light patterns the valley.

feed.title: Himalayas from Ranikhet

image.credit: Harshit SR / UnpetitproleX, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ranikhet is a hill station and cantonment in Almora district, Uttarakhand, about 1,869 metres above sea level. The British took Kumaon from the Gorkhas after the conquest of Almora in 1815, bought land here in 1868 and formed a cantonment the following year, when the Kumaon Regiment set up its headquarters. The town lies within sight of the western Himalayas, and this panorama, taken on 14 December 2020, lines up a chain of summits including Trisul at 7,120 metres, Nanda Devi at 7,817 metres, Nanda Kot at 6,861 metres and Panchachuli at 6,904 metres, the highest peak of its group.
feed.lookAt: A long, thin panorama suits a mountain chain. The white summits sit on a single horizontal band under blue sky, while the dark foothills fill the bottom half and give the ice its contrast. Notice how the winter air holds detail all the way to the farthest peak.

feed.title: Side shows at the Vermont state fair, Rutland

image.credit: Jack Delano, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jack Delano made this colour slide at the Vermont state fair in Rutland in September 1941. Born Yakov Ovcharov in the Russian Empire in 1914, he worked for the Farm Security Administration, the federal programme that sent photographers across the United States, and later settled in Puerto Rico, where he also composed music and made films. Here he looked down onto the midway from above: a Ferris wheel stands against a hillside of trees, a round tent topped by a flag sits in the centre, and signs for trick riders, a thrill show and a lion act line the far right, while a few visitors cross the dirt ground.
feed.lookAt: Delano shot from a raised vantage so tents, wheel and crowd stack in layers instead of overlapping. The big round roof anchors the centre, and the Ferris wheel's thin geometry fills the left. Climb a few metres when you shoot a busy scene and the clutter sorts itself.

caption.title: Side shows at the Vermont state fair, Rutland

feed.title: Karst peaks of Vang Vieng

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Vang Vieng is a city in Vientiane Province, Laos, on the Nam Song River, 130 kilometres north of the capital Vientiane. It was first settled around 1353 as a staging post between Luang Prabang and Vientiane, and was renamed Vang Vieng during French colonial rule in the 1890s. When Laos opened to tourism in the late 1990s, backpackers arrived for the limestone karst landscape and for tubing and kayaking on the river. This view looks north from the top of Mount Nam Xay at 6:19 on a sunny morning in the monsoon, on 22 June 2020, with mist still settled between the green peaks.
feed.lookAt: Low sun rakes across the karst and gives each tower a bright edge and a shadowed flank, so the peaks stack into layers. The mist in the valley adds a pale band between them. Shoot early in the monsoon season, when morning clearings give you both light and haze.

feed.title: Maniniaro / Angelus Peak

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Maniniaro, also called Angelus Peak, is a mountain in Nelson Lakes National Park, near the northwestern end of New Zealand's main divide. It is not the tallest peak in the Angelus Ridge or the wider Travers Range, but it is a popular tramping destination and is significant to the Ngāti Apa ki te Rā Tō iwi, whose beliefs link it with the nearby Rotomaninitua / Lake Angelus as the footprints of their ancestors. Angelus Hut stands on the lake shore and is the usual base for the summit. This panorama was made on 27 July 2019, in winter, when snow covers the basin.
feed.lookAt: Snow turns the basin into a clean white floor, so the dark rock ridges become a rhythm of triangles across the frame. A wide panorama keeps the mountain's scale honest. The heavy cloud on the right shades the slope and balances the bright peaks on the left.

caption.title: Maniniaro / Angelus Peak
caption.line2: Michal Klajban · Nelson Lakes National Park

feed.title: Flock in Owens Valley

image.credit: Ansel Adams, U.S. National Archives, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams made this photograph of a flock of sheep in Owens Valley in 1941. It belongs to the series Photographs of National Parks and Monuments, compiled in 1941 and 1942 and documenting the period from about 1933 to 1942. Adams was a landscape photographer and environmentalist who helped found Group f/64, which favoured sharp focus and the full tonal range, and he developed the Zone System with Fred Archer to control exposure and development. He was later contracted by the Department of the Interior to photograph national parks. Here the sheep fill most of the frame, with a dark animal at the back and distant mountains on the horizon.
feed.lookAt: The sheep cover the frame edge to edge, so the pattern of wool does the work, and a thin strip of mountains and sky sits at the top for place. The one darker animal near the back breaks the repeat. Wait for a gap in the crowd to make a focal point.

feed.title: Hubbard Glacier

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Hubbard Glacier lies in Wrangell–St. Elias National Park and Preserve in eastern Alaska and extends into Kluane National Park and Reserve in Yukon, Canada. It is named for Gardiner Hubbard. Its longest source begins 122 kilometres from its snout, and ice takes about 400 years to travel the full length of the glacier. Because the glacier is advancing, it blocked the outlet of Russell Fjord in 1986. Diego Delso made this panorama on 20 August 2017, looking across the water at the ice front under a lid of grey cloud, with snowy mountains rising behind it.
feed.lookAt: Overcast sky flattens the light, which suits ice: the blue-white wall keeps its detail instead of blowing out. The still water doubles it as a pale band. Put the horizon low and let the cloud and mountains weigh down the top of a long, thin frame.

feed.title: Sunbeams in the Bryant Range

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Bryant Range is a range of low mountains in the northern South Island of New Zealand.
