feed.lookAt: The long beak, folded wings and looping tail are drawn by thin pale lines on plain, evenly textured ground. A flat subject needs a quiet background, and here the dull desert lets a few fine lines carry the whole picture. Shoot straight down from above so the figure keeps its true outline.

feed.title: Strokkur erupting

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Strokkur is a fountain-type geyser in a geothermal area beside the Hvítá River in the southwest of Iceland, east of Reykjavík. Its name is Icelandic for churn. It typically erupts every six to ten minutes, and its usual height is 15 to 20 metres, although it can sometimes reach 40 metres. Diego Delso photographed an eruption in the Haukadalur geothermal area on 16 August 2014 at 13:21. In this frame the white column has just risen from a pale blue pool of water, and a small group of visitors stands on the pale ground at the right, watching it.
feed.lookAt: Because Strokkur erupts every few minutes, you can watch one go off, then frame and wait for the next. Here the column rises into a large empty sky, and the small people at the edge show how tall it is. Leave open space above the peak.

feed.title: Artist's Palette, Death Valley

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith is an American photographer and author, born in 1946, whose work documents the landscapes, architecture and people of the rural and urban United States in a nationwide study in progress since the 1980s. She has donated her photographs to the Library of Congress since 1992, creating a collection of nearly 100,000 images, all in the public domain. This frame shows Artist's Palette, a formation featuring multi-colored layers of rock within Death Valley National Park in California. Exif data records that it was taken on 20 December 2012, in the afternoon. Green, white and tan slopes sit under a bare brown ridge and a cloudless blue sky.
feed.lookAt: Low winter sun lifts the blue-green and pale layers out of the brown hillside, and the cloudless sky leaves nothing to compete. When the colour is the subject, keep the frame simple. Look for side light on slopes, and a lens that fills the frame with layered rock.

caption.title: Artist's Palette, Death Valley
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Sossusvlei, looking south

image.credit: Hans Hillewaert, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Sossusvlei is a salt and clay pan surrounded by high red dunes in the southern part of the Namib Desert, in the Namib-Naukluft National Park of Namibia. Its name is of mixed origin: vlei is the Afrikaans word for marsh, and sossus is Nama for no return or dead end. The pan is an endorheic drainage basin, meaning it has no outflow, for the ephemeral Tsauchab River. Hans Hillewaert made this panorama looking south on 14 June 2007. A dune crest in the foreground sweeps from the left into a lit red slope, and the pan and distant ridges stretch beyond it under a clear blue sky.
feed.lookAt: The sharp crest of the foreground dune runs diagonally into the frame and leads the eye out to the distant ridges. In a wide panorama, give the eye a path like this one. A near ridge also sets the scale of everything behind it.

facts: Salt and clay pan among high red dunes

feed.title: Cass Saddle, Craigieburn

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Craigieburn Forest Park is a protected area in the South Island of New Zealand, next to Arthur's Pass National Park. It was established in 1967, covers 44,694.78 hectares of mostly mountainous terrain, and is administered by the Department of Conservation. Beech forest covers the lower areas, and native tussock and other ground-covering plants dominate higher up. The Cass-Lagoon Saddle track crosses Cass Saddle, which stands at 1,326 metres. Michal Klajban took this panorama from that track on 25 November 2019, looking at the mountains to the north-west, mostly the Black Range. Dark forest fills the valley, and snow lies in streaks on the peaks.
feed.lookAt: Tussock in the foreground, dark forest in the valley and snow on the ridges build three layers of depth. Compose in layers like this on a mountain trail, so a wide scene does not flatten. Find a tilted foreground slope to lead into it.

feed.title: Marchers at the 45th anniversary of the Selma march

image.credit: Carol M. Highsmith, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carol M. Highsmith is an American photographer and author who has donated her photographs to the Library of Congress since 1992. Her nationwide project documents the landscapes, architecture and people of the United States. This picture belongs to The George F. Landegger Collection of Alabama Photographs in Carol M. Highsmith's America. It shows the 45th anniversary of the 1965 Civil Rights March from Selma to Montgomery, Alabama, when people gathered to walk across the Edmund Pettus Bridge to recreate the event. Exif data records that it was taken on 7 March 2010. A line of marchers stands arm in arm across a wide street, with older brick storefronts and traffic lights behind them.
feed.lookAt: A line of people filling the width of the road, shot from street level and straight on, turns a crowd into a single wall of faces. Hold a moment like this at eye level, with a wide lens, and wait until the line holds still before you press the shutter.

caption.title: Marchers at the 45th anniversary of the Selma march
caption.line2: Carol M. Highsmith · Library of Congress

feed.title: Christchurch Art Gallery at blue hour

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Christchurch Art Gallery, in Māori Te Puna o Waiwhetū, is the public art gallery of the city of Christchurch, New Zealand. It has its own substantial art collection and also presents a programme of New Zealand and international exhibitions. It is funded by Christchurch City Council. The gallery opened on 10 May 2003, replacing the Robert McDougall Art Gallery, which had opened in 1932. Michal Klajban photographed it during the blue hour on 22 April 2019. In this panorama a curved glass front bends around the entrance, and it reflects the blue-grey evening sky above a paved square.
feed.lookAt: At blue hour the sky and the glass match in colour, so the building's curved facade reads as one soft shape. Shoot soon after sunset, while the sky still holds light, to get this balance. Use the reflections as a second layer of detail.

caption.title: Christchurch Art Gallery at blue hour

feed.title: Lille Lungegårdsvannet, Bergen

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Lille Lungegårdsvannet, also called Smålungeren, is a small lake of about five acres in the centre of the city of Bergen in Vestland county, Norway. The octagonal lake is natural and was historically connected to the nearby Store Lungegårdsvannet bay by a short strait, but the strait was filled in 1926. Today the lake lies in a park in the city centre, and a large decorative fountain stands in its middle. Diego Delso photographed this panorama on 8 September 2019. A wooded hillside covered with houses rises behind the water, and the fountain throws a white plume into the still lake.
feed.lookAt: A very wide panorama can hold the whole story of a city: water, fountain, park, houses and hillside in one frame. Place a bright focal point such as the fountain near the middle so the eye has an anchor. Stitch frames on a level tripod.

feed.title: Absinthe House entrance, New Orleans

image.credit: Arnold Genthe, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arnold Genthe, born in 1869 and died in 1942, was a German-American photographer, best known for his photographs of Northern California, San Francisco's Chinatown, the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, and his portraits of noted people. The Library of Congress holds this negative, titled Absinthe House entrance, New Orleans, and dates it between 1920 and 1926. The frame shows an arched double door with a grille above it, and a balcony with ironwork brackets overhead. A drainpipe runs down the stained plaster wall, and scratches mark the surface of the old negative.
feed.lookAt: Straight on, the arched door sits in the middle and the balcony's dark shadow caps it like a lid. Fill the frame with one doorway to make a tidy, symmetrical picture. Notice the stained wall, the grille's pattern and the drainpipe, which add age.

feed.title: Sacsayhuamán walls

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Sacsayhuamán is a citadel on the northern outskirts of Cusco, Peru, the historic capital of the Inca Empire, at an altitude of 3,701 metres. The Killke culture built the first sections around 1100, and the Inca expanded it from the 13th century. Dry stone walls of huge stones were built there, with workers carefully cutting the boulders to fit them together tightly without mortar. In 1983, Cusco and Sacsayhuamán together were designated as sites on the UNESCO World Heritage List. Diego Delso photographed a row of the wall's corners on 31 July 2015, at about ten in the morning, under a deep blue sky.
feed.lookAt: Sunlight from the side picks out every joint between the stones, and the zigzag line of corners marches into the distance. When photographing masonry, wait for raking light and use the repeating angles as rhythm. The deep blue sky gives the grey stone a clean edge.

feed.title: Upsala Glacier from orbit

image.credit: NASA Expedition 21 crew, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Southern Patagonian Icefield of Argentina and Chile is the southern remnant of the Patagonia Ice Sheet that covered the southern Andes during the last ice age. Upsala Glacier is a large valley glacier on the icefield's eastern side, in Los Glaciares National Park. Its name comes from the old spelling of Uppsala University, which sponsored the first glaciological studies there. The NASA Expedition 21 crew photographed it on 25 October 2009, during spring in the Southern Hemisphere, with a Nikon D2Xs and a 400 mm lens. Icebergs were calving from the glacier terminus into Lago Argentino. Turquoise lakes lie among brown rock beside the white ice.
feed.lookAt: From orbit, ice, rock and turquoise water become abstract patches of colour and texture. A long lens compresses the view so the glacier's flow lines read as a pattern. Look for strong colour contrast, like the turquoise lakes against dark brown, when you shoot from above.

caption.title: Upsala Glacier from orbit
caption.line2: NASA Expedition 21 crew · Santa Cruz Province, Patagonia

feed.title: Troops marching along a city street, China

image.credit: Arthur Rothstein, Library of Congress, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Arthur Rothstein was an American photographer, born on 17 July 1915 and died on 11 November 1985. His career spanned five decades, and he received recognition as one of America's premier photojournalists. The Library of Congress catalogues this 1946 picture as a view from above of provincial troops marching along a city street in the Jiangsu Province or Yunnan Province in China. Rows of soldiers fill the left side of the frame and move down a cobbled street. A crowd of onlookers lines the right side, and a man on horseback appears at the bottom. The catalogue does not name the city.
feed.lookAt: A high vantage point turns the column into a pattern of repeated hats and heads. The diagonal cobbled street leads the eye, and the horseman at the bottom gives scale. Find an upstairs window or a rooftop over a street to show a crowd as a whole.

caption.title: Troops marching along a city street, China

feed.title: Verkhoyansk Range from the air

image.credit: Ilya Varlamov, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Verkhoyansk Range is a mountain range in the Sakha Republic, Russia, near the settlement of Verkhoyansk, which is known for its frigid climate. It is part of the East Siberian Mountains and lies just west of the boundary of the Eurasian and North American tectonic plates. The mountains were formed by folding and represent an anticline. The range was covered by glaciers during the Last Glacial Period, and the northern section, such as the Orulgan Range, shows typical Alpine relief. Ilya Varlamov took this aerial view on 28 February 2019. Low light turns the snowy ridges orange against the dark valley, and a river winds across the distant floor.
feed.lookAt: Low, warm light touches only the tops of the ridges, so the dark valleys fall into shadow and the shapes stand out. For aerial mountain shots, fly when the sun is near the horizon. Expose for the lit slopes and let the shadows go dark.

feed.title: Alicudi from the south

image.credit: Carsten Steger, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Alicudi is the westernmost of the seven islands that make up the Aeolian archipelago, a volcanic island chain north of Sicily. The island is about 40 kilometres west of Lipari, is roughly circular, and has a total area of 5.2 square kilometres. It was formed by the long-extinct Montagnola volcano about 150,000 years ago, and its highest point is 675 metres. Pirate raids were frequent for centuries, which led residents to build their houses on high terraces. Carsten Steger took this aerial image on 22 May 2022, looking from the south. The cone sits alone in deep blue sea, with small white houses on its slope.
feed.lookAt: A single shape on a plain background makes a strong picture. The island's triangle sits slightly off centre in deep blue water, and the tiny houses give its scale. When you shoot a lone subject from the air, choose a clean background and keep it uncluttered.

feed.title: Pine Cone and Eucalyptus Leaves

image.credit: Ansel Adams, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ansel Adams was an American landscape photographer and environmentalist, known for his black-and-white images of the American West. He helped found Group f/64, an association of photographers advocating pure photography, which favoured sharp focus and the use of the full tonal range of a photograph. He and Fred Archer developed the Zone System, a method of achieving a desired final print through a technical understanding of how the tonal range is the result of choices made in exposure, negative development and printing. At age 14, he was given his first camera during his first visit to Yosemite National Park. This picture, Pine Cone and Eucalyptus Leaves, dates from 1932.
feed.lookAt: The cone's overlapping scales are sharp from edge to edge, and the curved leaves around it repeat its soft diagonals. Move in close to an object on the ground and keep everything in focus, using a small aperture and a tripod, so that its texture becomes the picture.

feed.title: Koppelpoort, Amersfoort

image.credit: Bert, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Koppelpoort is a medieval gate in the Dutch city of Amersfoort, in the province of Utrecht. It was built between 1380 and 1425 as part of Amersfoort's second city wall, which was completed around 1450, and it combines land and water gates. It was attacked in 1427 during a siege of the city, and the attack was repelled. Pierre Cuypers restored it in 1885 and 1886, giving it its current appearance. A puppet theatre was housed in the gate from 1969 to 1993. Bert took this photograph on 5 August 2008. Brick towers with pointed slate roofs stand beside an arched water gate that is reflected in calm water.
feed.lookAt: Still water doubles the gate and fills the lower half of the frame with its reflection. Look for a calm canal or moat and shoot from the bank so the arch reads as a full circle. Include the arched structure on the left to show how the gate joins the wall.

feed.title: Švihov Castle from the east

image.credit: Jiří Strašek, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Švihov Castle is a Gothic water castle in Švihov in the Plzeň Region of the Czech Republic. The Rýzmberk of Skála family built it, and it was rebuilt in 1480–1489 in the late Gothic style under Půta Švihovský of Rýzmberk. His sons continued the work and invited the architect Benedikt Rejt, who designed the moat system with massive horseshoe-shaped bastions, finished by 1520. The Czernin family held the castle until nationalisation in 1945. Jiří Strašek photographed it from the east on 1 September 2014, at about seven in the morning. Low sun lights the castle's orange roofs and pale walls, while the rough foreground lies in shade.
feed.lookAt: Early sun strikes the castle while the foreground stays in cold shade, so warm and cool colours sit together in one frame. Arrive at dawn, while the foreground is still in shade. Let the streaky clouds above fill the space and balance the dark mound.

feed.title: Boulevard Hotel neon sign

image.credit: Radomianin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Miami Beach Architectural District, also called the Miami Art Deco District, is a United States historic district designated in 1979 in the South Beach neighbourhood of Miami Beach, Florida. It contains 960 historic buildings and is bounded by the Atlantic Ocean to the east, Sixth Street to the south, Alton Road to the west and the Collins Canal and Dade Boulevard to the north. The Boulevard Hotel stands on Ocean Drive. The architect August Swarz designed it, and it was completed in 1950. The photographer Radomianin took this picture of its neon sign from the east on 25 August 2018, at night.
feed.lookAt: Glowing neon on a black night sky needs very little else. The red stepped outline frames the script sign and gives it a border. Expose for the neon, not the dark, so the tubes keep their colour instead of burning out to white.

facts: Ocean Drive, Miami Beach Art Deco District

feed.title: Stanford from the Oval

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Stanford University is a private research university in Stanford, California, United States. Railroad magnate Leland Stanford, then a United States senator and former governor of California, and his wife, Jane, founded it in 1885 in memory of their only child, Leland Stanford Jr., who died from typhoid at the age of 15. It admitted its first students in 1891. The university struggled financially after Leland died in 1893 and again after much of the campus was damaged by the 1906 San Francisco earthquake. King of Hearts took this panorama from the Oval on the morning of 7 May 2011. Red-tiled arcades and tall palms run along a long band of lawn.
feed.lookAt: The wide band of lawn and the low red-roofed buildings make a long horizontal stripe, and the palms break it with two vertical accents. A panorama suits subjects that are long and low. Shoot in early light, while it rakes along the arcades.

feed.title: Seljalandsfoss from behind

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Seljalandsfoss is a waterfall in the South Region of Iceland, right by Route 1 and the road to Þórsmörk. It drops 60 metres over the cliffs of the former coastline, and it is part of the Seljalandsá river, which has its origin in the volcano glacier Eyjafjallajökull. Visitors can walk behind the falls into a small cave. Diego Delso made this picture of the sunset from the back of the waterfall on 16 August 2014, at about ten at night. The cave's mossy rim forms a dark arch around the glowing evening sky.
feed.lookAt: The cave's rim frames the falls like a window, with the bright sky and spray inside a dark arch. Look for a natural frame like this to hold a scene. The brightness range is large, so expose for the sky and keep the cave dark.

facts: Visitors can walk behind the falls

feed.title: Gokyo Lake from Gokyo Ri

image.credit: Vyacheslav Argenberg, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Gokyo Lakes are oligotrophic lakes in Nepal's Sagarmatha National Park, at an elevation of 4,700–5,000 metres. They are named after the peak Gokyo Ri. In September 2007, Gokyo and its associated wetlands of 7,770 hectares were designated a Ramsar site. From the summit of Gokyo Ri, Ngozumpa glacier, the largest and longest glacier in the Himalayas, is right below, with commanding views over nearby Cholatse, Taboche, Kangtega, Thamserku and other peaks. Vyacheslav Argenberg took this picture on 16 October 2009. A turquoise lake lies below dark ridges, and two small figures stand on the rocks at lower right.
feed.lookAt: The bright turquoise lake is the one saturated colour in a scene of brown rock, white ice and blue sky, so it draws the eye first. Two tiny hikers on the slope give a sense of scale. Include people to show how big a mountain view is.

caption.title: Gokyo Lake from Gokyo Ri
caption.line2: Vyacheslav Argenberg · Sagarmatha National Park, Khumbu

feed.title: Khone Phapheng Falls

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Khone Falls and Pha Pheng Falls together form a waterfall in Champasak Province on the Mekong River in southern Laos, near the border with Cambodia. At 10,783 metres wide from one edge of its multiple channels to the other, it is the widest waterfall in the world. The falls are characterised by thousands of islands and countless waterways, which give the area its name, Si Phan Don, or the 4,000 islands. The highest falls reach 21 metres, and the average discharge is nearly 11,000 cubic metres per second. Basile Morin photographed them on 25 December 2019. White water pours between dark brown rocks, and a low forest line sits on the far bank.
feed.lookAt: Here the shutter is fast enough to keep texture in the foam instead of blurring it into silk. Choose your shutter speed for the effect you want. The brown rocks at right give the water something solid to flow around.

caption.title: Khone Phapheng Falls
caption.line2: Basile Morin · Si Phan Don, Champasak Province

feed.title: Wreck of HMS Justice, Ushuaia

image.credit: Gabriel Resende Veiga, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: HMS Justice was a Royal Navy rescue tug, built in the United States as the rescue tug ATR-20 and launched on 18 October 1943. It was transferred to the Royal Navy under Lend-Lease and commissioned in April 1944. After the war it was returned to the U.S. Navy and sold for commercial service, and in 1947 it was renamed St. Christopher. After engine and rudder problems in 1954, it was laid up at Ushuaia, Argentina, and beached and abandoned there in 1957. Gabriel Resende Veiga photographed the wreck on 22 May 2017, around midday. The hull sits low in still water, and its white wheelhouse is reflected below it.
feed.lookAt: Calm water doubles the wreck, and the hull's dark line splits the frame into the ship above and its reflection below. Shoot at water level in still conditions. The blue sky and soft cloud keep the white wheelhouse clean and bright.

caption.title: Wreck of HMS Justice, Ushuaia
caption.line2: Gabriel Resende Veiga · Ushuaia, Tierra del Fuego

feed.title: 151 Cambridge Terrace at dusk

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: 151 Cambridge Terrace, also known as the Deloitte Building, is a contemporary office building in central Christchurch, New Zealand, on the Avon River at the corner of Cambridge Terrace and Gloucester Street. Jasmax designed it, and it was completed in 2014 as one of the earliest commercial projects in the city after the 2011 Christchurch earthquake. It is the first building in New Zealand to use Triple Pendulum base isolation. Its curved, undulating exterior is wrapped in blue-tinted glass fins. Michal Klajban photographed it during the blue hour on 28 April 2019. Lit floors glow warm gold behind the glass, and streaks of car lights cross the street at the bottom.
feed.lookAt: Warm lit windows against a cool blue sky is a colour contrast that works best at blue hour. The curved fins catch the light in rows, and a slow exposure turns passing cars into red streaks along the street. Use a tripod and a few seconds.

facts: First in New Zealand with Triple Pendulum base isolation

feed.title: Rain Vortex at night, Jewel Changi

image.credit: Timothy A. Gonsalves, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Jewel Changi Airport is a nature-themed entertainment and retail complex linked to Terminals 1, 2 and 3 of Changi Airport, at the eastern end of Singapore. Its centrepiece is the Rain Vortex, the world's tallest indoor waterfall, set inside a terraced forest. The complex covers 135,700 square metres across ten storeys, five above ground and five in the basement. In October 2019, six months after its soft opening, it welcomed 50 million visitors, and in 2024 it reached a record of more than 80 million. Timothy A. Gonsalves photographed the vortex at night on 14 February 2023, when the glass-and-steel dome overhead is lit in green and the falling water glows from within.
feed.lookAt: The photographer stood back and shot upward, so the triangular dome frames the glowing column of water like a funnel. Lights are the subject here: a single saturated colour against darker foliage. At night, look for one bright source and let everything else fall into shadow.

facts: Rain Vortex, the world's tallest indoor waterfall

caption.title: Rain Vortex at night, Jewel Changi

feed.title: Kuang Si Falls and its emerald pools

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kuang Si Falls, also written Kuang Xi, is a multi-tiered waterfall in Laos about 29 kilometres south of the town of Luang Prabang. The water begins in shallow pools atop a steep hillside and runs down to the main fall, which drops 60 metres. The falls are a favourite side trip for visitors to Luang Prabang, and the journey from the town's night market takes about 53 minutes. Basile Morin photographed the emerald pools on 27 January 2022, in the late afternoon. In this frame the water slows into terraces of pale green before it spills over a small stone lip into the next pool.
feed.lookAt: Notice how the falling water is softened into silky threads while the leaves and rock stay sharp. That is a slow shutter speed, often half a second or longer. Brace the camera on a tripod or a rock, lower the ISO and use a neutral density filter in daylight.

facts: About 29 km south of Luang Prabang

caption.title: Kuang Si Falls and its emerald pools

feed.title: Mount Ararat above the Araratian plain

image.credit: Serouj Ourishian, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Mount Ararat, officially Mount Ağrı and also known as Masis, is a snow-capped, dormant compound volcano in easternmost Turkey. It has two cones: Greater Ararat, at 5,137 metres the highest peak in Turkey and the Armenian highlands, and Little Ararat at 3,896 metres. The massif is about 35 kilometres wide at its base. The first recorded ascent was made in 1829 by Friedrich Parrot, Khachatur Abovian and four others. Though it lies outside the borders of modern Armenia, the mountain is the country's principal national symbol and is shown on its coat of arms. Serouj Ourishian stitched two images into this wide view, taken on 3 November 2016, with the Khor Virap monastery at centre left.
feed.lookAt: A wide stitched panorama needs a calm base. Here the ruled lines of the plain run flat across the lower third and lead toward the twin white peaks, which sit at the horizon. Keep the horizon level, give the sky a clear half, and let one distant landmark anchor the scene.

place.region: Ağrı, with the Araratian plain in the foreground

caption.title: Mount Ararat above the Araratian plain
caption.line2: Serouj Ourishian · Ağrı, with the Araratian plain in the foreground

feed.title: Pancuran Tujuh hot spring

image.credit: Crisco 1492, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Pancuran Tujuh, Javanese for Seven Springs, is a hot spring on the slopes of Mount Slamet in Baturraden District, Banyumas, Central Java. According to local legend, it was discovered by a Muslim missionary known as Mbah Atas Angin. Its sulfuric waters are considered to have healing properties. Crisco 1492 photographed the spring on 23 March 2015, in the late morning. Mineral deposits have built a stepped yellow and orange fan where the water spills out, and a small hut stands among tree roots and dense green foliage just above it. The tropical forest closes in around the stream on every side.
feed.lookAt: The yellow-orange mineral fan is the only warm colour in a frame of green. Stand low, close to the deposit, and the steps lead the eye up to the tiny hut, which tells you the scale. Include a human-made object to show how large the landscape really is.

feed.title: Prambanan temple compound

image.credit: CEphoto, Uwe Aranas, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Prambanan is a 9th-century Hindu temple compound in the Special Region of Yogyakarta, in southern Java, about 17 kilometres northeast of the city of Yogyakarta. It is dedicated to the Trimūrti: Brahma the Creator, Vishnu the Preserver and Shiva the Destroyer. A UNESCO World Heritage Site, it is the largest Hindu temple site in Indonesia and the second largest in Southeast Asia after Angkor Wat. The compound originally consisted of 240 temple structures, and its central building is 47 metres high. Uwe Aranas photographed the surviving towers on 5 February 2015, beneath a bright overcast sky, with green grass in the foreground.
feed.lookAt: The temples' dark, pointed towers repeat at different heights, forming a rhythm across the frame. An overcast sky turns the stone into a silhouette and keeps the clouds from competing. Use a longer lens to compress the towers together, and look for repetition when you photograph architecture.

feed.title: Asahi headquarters and Skytree at blue hour

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Sumida is a special ward of the Tokyo Metropolis in Japan, with an estimated population of 287,766 as of 1 April 2025 and a density of 20,120 people per square kilometre. Its city office is in Azumabashi, and its commercial centre is around Kinshicho Station. This view looks across the Sumida River from the wharf near Azuma Bridge. Basile Morin photographed it on 16 June 2019 at blue hour with a full moon. The frame includes the Asahi Breweries headquarters, the Asahi Flame designed by Philippe Starck on top of the Asahi Beer Hall, and the Tokyo Skytree.
feed.lookAt: Blue hour gives a sky that still has colour and a city that has switched on its lights. Here the deep blue sky holds a small pale moon, and the golden flame echoes the glass tower beside it. Arrive early, and use a tripod to keep the river reflections sharp.

caption.title: Asahi headquarters and Skytree at blue hour

feed.title: Mekong sandbar at Si Phan Don

image.credit: Basile Morin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Si Phan Don, meaning 4,000 islands, is a riverine archipelago in the Mekong River in Champasak Province, southern Laos. Half of its islands are submerged when the river is in flood. The principal islands are Don Khong, Don Som, Don Det and Don Khon. The area holds the remains of the first railway in Laos, a narrow gauge line built by the French to bypass the Khone Phapheng Falls, a series of impassable rapids. Basile Morin photographed this Mekong beach near the island of Don Loppadi at sunset on 28 December 2017, as three children returned to their boat.
feed.lookAt: The sandbar curves away like a long line, drawing you toward the small figures wading beside the green boat. They give scale and a story. Wait for the moment when people enter the frame at the right spot, and keep them small against the sky and water.

facts: Don Khong, Don Som, Don Det, Don Khon

caption.title: Mekong sandbar at Si Phan Don

feed.title: Hohllay rock cave, Berdorf

image.credit: Dietmar Rabich, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Hohllay, or Huel Lee, is a rock formation near Berdorf in the Little Switzerland area of Luxembourg's Gutland region. The name means hollow rock, and it describes a man-made hollowed stone with narrow passages and caves. Its history dates back to Roman times, when stones were quarried here for buildings, and quarrying continued in the Middle Ages. Berdorf itself is a small town in eastern Luxembourg known for the sandstone rocks around it. Dietmar Rabich photographed the interior on 23 May 2015, in late afternoon, looking out through the arches toward green forest.
feed.lookAt: The photographer sat inside the dark cave and let the arches frame the bright forest beyond. The sandstone ceiling is textured by the light along its edge. When you shoot from the shadows toward the light, expose for the bright part and let the foreground go dark.

feed.title: Wahkeena Falls in October

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Wahkeena Falls is a 242-foot waterfall in the Columbia River Gorge in Oregon. Unlike nearby Multnomah Falls, its water does not plunge directly to the ground but has a more subtle cascading flow. The name is an English transliteration of a phrase reportedly from the Yakama language meaning most beautiful. The falls lie along the Historic Columbia River Highway, about 13 miles east of Troutdale, and a short walk from the parking lot leads to the stone bridge. King of Hearts photographed the stream on 31 October 2019, with fallen autumn leaves along its banks.
feed.lookAt: Water is turned into a smooth ribbon, which means a slow shutter, while the leaves stay still. The vertical frame follows the stream from bottom to top. Shoot waterfalls in shade or overcast light, set a low ISO and use a tripod, and count the exposure in fractions of a second.

caption.title: Wahkeena Falls in October
caption.line2: King of Hearts · Columbia River Gorge, Oregon

feed.title: The Great Bath, Roman Baths

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Roman Baths are well-preserved thermae in the city of Bath, Somerset, England. A temple was built on the site between 60 and 70 AD, in the first decades of Roman Britain, and its presence led to the small Roman settlement of Aquae Sulis. The baths were designed for public bathing and used until the end of Roman rule in Britain in the 5th century. The area was redeveloped several times in the Middle Ages, and all buildings at street level date from the 19th century. Diego Delso photographed the Great Bath on 12 August 2014, in the evening, using HDR.
feed.lookAt: The still, green water doubles the colonnade and sky in a mirror image, with the horizon cutting the picture in half. Shoot a low reflection straight on, so that both halves match. Calm water and symmetry give a simple, strong composition.

feed.title: Serranía de Hornocal

image.credit: Havardtl, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Serranía de Hornocal is a mountain range 25 kilometres from the city of Humahuaca, in the Argentine province of Jujuy. Exposed in the range is a limestone formation called Yacoraite, which extends from Salta through the Quebrada de Humahuaca and the Bolivian Altiplano to Peru. The mountains reach 4,761 metres above sea level. The Quebrada de Humahuaca was declared a World Heritage Site in 2003 for its colourful mountain landscapes and for the historic Inca caravan road that runs through it. Havardtl photographed the folded red, pink and brown bands close up on 18 August 2017, under a clear blue sky.
feed.lookAt: A clear blue sky makes the striped ridges look even more saturated. Fill the frame with the colour bands and leave a thin strip of sky, so the folds become a pattern. A long lens from a distance flattens the slopes and shows how the strata are folded.

feed.title: Travis Wetland panorama

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Travis Wetland is a wetland in the suburb of Burwood in Christchurch, New Zealand, with an ecological restoration programme under way. It covers 116 hectares of land that was formerly drained and used as a dairy farm, and in 2009 it won the Urban Sustainability category of the Green Ribbon Awards. The Māori name for the area is Ōruapaeroa, and before European occupation it was rich with eels and bird life and was an important food-gathering place for the local iwi, Ngāi Tahu. Michal Klajban photographed this wide panorama on 15 August 2019, and several bird species can be seen when it is zoomed in.
feed.lookAt: This very wide panorama holds thin bands of sky, water and reeds, and only on zooming in do the birds appear. Choose a long, low format when the subject is a horizon. Then add small details, such as birds, that reward the viewer who looks closely.

feed.title: Radcliffe Camera from St Mary's tower

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Radcliffe Camera is a University of Oxford building designed by James Gibbs in a Baroque style and built in 1737 to 1749 to house a library. It later became a reading room of the Bodleian Library. It stands south of the Old Bodleian and north of the Church of St Mary the Virgin, between Brasenose College and All Souls College. Its circular form and its separation from other buildings make it the focal point of the University, and it is almost always included in visual shorthand for Oxford. Diliff photographed it from the tower of St Mary's on 15 October 2006, as a ten-segment panorama.
feed.lookAt: Shot from above, the round building and its lawn become a clear central shape against the roofs of Oxford. A higher viewpoint can separate a landmark from its surroundings. Look for towers, bridges and hills, and use a short telephoto to keep the subject large.

caption.title: Radcliffe Camera from St Mary's tower

feed.title: Upper Belvedere at blue hour

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Belvedere is a historic building complex and art museum in Vienna, Austria, made up of two Baroque palaces, the Upper and Lower Belvedere, together with the Orangery, the Palace Stables and a formal garden. It stands in the third district, Landstraße, on the south-eastern edge of the historic centre. It was built as the summer residence of Prince Eugene of Savoy, designed principally by Johann Lukas von Hildebrandt, and finished in the early 18th century. Diego Delso photographed the Upper Belvedere at blue hour on 1 February 2020, as the lit facade doubled in the still water of the pond.
feed.lookAt: At blue hour the sky still holds deep colour, and the palace's warm lights stand out against it. The still pond repeats them as a long golden streak. Shoot just after sunset, from a low viewpoint, and use a tripod so the reflection stays sharp.

facts: Part of the Historic Centre of Vienna World Heritage Site

feed.title: Silfra fissure, Þingvellir

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Silfra is a canyon within Þingvellir National Park in Iceland, a rift between the North American and Eurasian tectonic plates. The park lies in a rift valley that marks the crest of the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, about 40 kilometres northeast of Reykjavík. Þingvellir was the site of the Alþing, Iceland's annual parliament, from the year 930 until 1798. The national park was founded in 1930, marking the 1,000th anniversary of the Althing, and it became a World Heritage Site in 2004. Diego Delso photographed snorkelers in the narrow canyon on 16 August 2014, in the late morning.
feed.lookAt: The tiny swimmers show you how narrow and deep the rift is. They stay small, and the rock walls frame them on both sides. Add a person to show scale in a large landscape, and shoot from a point where the lines of the walls lead to them.

facts: Rift between the North American and Eurasian plates

caption.title: Silfra fissure, Þingvellir
caption.line2: Diego Delso · Þingvellir National Park, Southern Region

feed.title: Lake Louise from the Beehive

image.credit: Chensiyuan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Lake Louise is a glacial lake in Banff National Park, Alberta, Canada, 5 kilometres west of the community of Lake Louise. The Stoney Nakoda people knew it as Lake of the Little Fishes. In 1882 Thomas Edmonds Wilson, led there by a Stoney Nakoda guide named Edwin Hunter, became the first non-Indigenous person to visit, and he first called it Emerald Lake. It was later named for Princess Louise Caroline Alberta. Its turquoise colour comes from rock flour carried in by meltwater from the glaciers above, and its surface is 0.8 square kilometres. Chensiyuan photographed this panorama from the Beehive in June 2019.
feed.lookAt: The raised viewpoint shows the lake's colour as a strip between the dark forest and the snowy mountain. A high vantage point helps you describe a landscape's shape. Look for a trail or lookout, and let a foreground edge frame the view.

feed.title: Hôtel des Invalides at twilight

image.credit: DXR, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Hôtel des Invalides, commonly called Les Invalides, is a complex of buildings in the 7th arrondissement of Paris, France, containing museums and monuments relating to the military history of France, as well as a hospital and an old soldiers' retirement home, its original purpose. It houses the Musée de l'Armée and the Cathedral of Saint-Louis-des-Invalides. Next to it is the Royal Chapel known as the Dôme des Invalides, the tallest church building in Paris at 107 metres, which holds the tomb of Napoleon. DXR photographed the north facade at twilight on 2 April 2014.
feed.lookAt: The long facade is perfectly symmetrical, the central dome sits on the road's vanishing line and the lamps run in matching rows. Stand on the central axis, level the camera, and let the road lead to the building. Symmetry works best when you are exactly on the centre line.

facts: Hospital and retirement home for soldiers

feed.title: Palácio do Planalto reflections

image.credit: Jonas Richter, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Palácio do Planalto in Brasília is the official workplace of the president of Brazil. Oscar Niemeyer designed it in 1958, and it was inaugurated on 21 April 1960. It stands on the Praça dos Três Poderes, east of the National Congress and across from the Supreme Federal Court. The president, vice-president and chief of staff work there, and the name Planalto is often used to mean the executive branch of the federal government. The modernist building is part of the Brasília World Heritage Site, designated by UNESCO in 1987. Jonas Richter photographed it on 27 September 2015, in late afternoon, with the building reflected in a pool.
feed.lookAt: A vertical frame, clean lines and a pool: the white columns and glass are repeated in warm reflections in the water below. When photographing modern architecture, look for reflecting water, keep verticals straight and wait for low sun to colour the glass.

feed.title: Laguna Miscanti

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Laguna Miscanti is a brackish lake in the Altiplano of the Antofagasta Region in northern Chile, with an area of about 13 square kilometres and the shape of an arrowhead. It has no permanent surface inflows or outflows apart from several springs. The lake lies among the volcanoes of the Central Andes in Los Flamencos National Reserve and is separated from the smaller Laguna Miñiques by a lava flow. It formed about 22,000 years ago and reformed 3,400 years ago after a dry spell. Diego Delso photographed the view in a very wide panorama on 8 February 2016.
feed.lookAt: Pale water, a yellow plain and brown volcanoes form three long bands under a cloudy sky. A panorama like this is only possible when nothing crosses the horizon. The road at each edge leads you into the picture. Choose a long, thin crop when the scene is a stripe.

facts: Brackish lake in Los Flamencos National Reserve

feed.title: Rock Arch and Spitzkoppe

image.credit: Daniel Kraft, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Spitzkoppe, from the German for pointed dome, is a group of bald granite peaks, or inselbergs, in the Namib desert of Namibia between Usakos and Swakopmund. The granite is more than 120 million years old, and the highest outcrop rises about 1,728 metres above sea level, around 670 metres above the plain. It is also called the Matterhorn of Namibia. Many examples of Bushmen artwork can be seen painted on the rock. Daniel Kraft photographed the Rock Arch with the main peak behind it on 24 May 2019, around midday, in a panorama with an even sky.
feed.lookAt: The arch is close, warm and large, while the pointed peak waits in the haze behind it. Photographing a near and a far landmark together shows how they relate. Keep both in the same frame, and use a wide lens so the foreground rock leads to the mountain.

place.region: Namib desert, between Usakos and Swakopmund
facts: Granite, more than 120 million years old

caption.title: Rock Arch and Spitzkoppe
caption.line2: Daniel Kraft · Namib desert, between Usakos and Swakopmund

feed.title: Rubin Observatory in the snow

image.credit: NOIRLab/NSF/AURA, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Vera C. Rubin Observatory, formerly the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope, is an astronomical observatory in the Coquimbo Region of Chile. It stands on El Peñón peak of Cerro Pachón, a mountain 2,682 metres high, while its base facility is about 100 kilometres away in La Serena. It is named for Vera Rubin, an American astronomer who pioneered discoveries about galactic rotation rates. The Simonyi Survey Telescope has an 8.4-metre primary mirror, and its camera is a 3.2-gigapixel sensor. This image from NOIRLab shows the observatory during a snowy day on Cerro Pachón.
feed.lookAt: Snow dusts the dark rock on the ridge while low sunlight turns the clouds gold. A small structure on the far skyline gives the huge mountain scale. Bad weather can be a good ally: wait for light to break through, and expose for the highlights so the snow keeps its texture.

feed.title: Paniri volcano and the San Pedro River

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Paniri is a stratovolcano in El Loa Province in the Antofagasta Region of Chile, near the Bolivian border. The name is Aymara for he who comes, visits. It is 5,960 metres high, with three craters, and lava flows are well preserved on its south-southwest flanks. Its youngest stage has been dated to about 150,000 years ago. The San Pedro de Inacaliri River is 76 kilometres long and ends in the Loa River, in an extremely dry region. Diego Delso photographed the river with the volcano behind it on 9 February 2016, in the early afternoon.
feed.lookAt: The river bends from the lower left into the middle of the frame, and the green moss on its bed is the brightest colour in a dry world. Use a winding stream as a leading line, and put the mountain at the end so that the eye travels from foreground to peak.

caption.title: Paniri volcano and the San Pedro River
caption.line2: Diego Delso · El Loa Province, Antofagasta Region

feed.title: Belvedere of Embodying Benevolence, Forbidden City

image.credit: Ermell, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Belvedere of Embodying Benevolence, called Tiren Ge in Chinese and also known as the Tiren Library, is a building in the Outer Court of the Forbidden City in Beijing, China. Its name has a Manchu form as well as a Chinese one, a reminder that the palace complex worked in more than one language. Ermell photographed it on 18 October 2007. The picture shows the hall from the front across the open paved courtyard: a double roof of golden tiles above red walls, a white balustrade along the base, and a small crowd of visitors dwarfed by the scale of the architecture around them.
feed.lookAt: Look at the symmetry: the hall sits dead centre, with the doors, the two roof tiers and the balustrade all mirroring left and right. Straight-on, square framing makes a formal building feel calm. The tiny visitors at the bottom give the viewer an instant sense of scale.

facts: Outer Court of the Forbidden City

caption.title: Belvedere of Embodying Benevolence, Forbidden City

feed.title: Sunrise over Huitzila, Hidalgo

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Huitzila is a locality in the municipality of Tizayuca, in the state of Hidalgo in central-eastern Mexico. It lies in the Tizayuca Valley and is part of Greater Mexico City. Diego Delso photographed this sunrise landscape on 10 October 2013, and the file page describes it simply as a sunrise in Huitzila. The wide, low frame follows the horizon: a row of dark trees stands in the middle ground, soft ridges of hills rise behind them in layers of haze, and the sun is just clearing the skyline at the right-hand edge, turning the sky from pale yellow to a gentle orange.
feed.lookAt: Look at the haze: each ridge is lighter than the one in front of it, which gives depth without any dramatic subject. Shoot toward the sun early, when the air is still hazy, and keep the sun at the edge of the frame so it adds warmth but does not blow out the scene.

feed.title: The Colosseum at dusk, Rome

image.credit: Diliff, CC BY-SA 2.5, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Rome is the capital and largest city of Italy, in the Lazio region, and its history spans 28 centuries. Roman mythology dates the founding of the city to around 753 BC, though the site has been inhabited for much longer. It is often called the City of Seven Hills and the Eternal City. This picture shows the Colosseum at dusk. Diliff made it on 30 April 2007 as a 4×4 segment panorama, shot with a Canon 5D and a 50mm f/1.8 lens at f/5.6. The lit stone glows orange against a deep blue sky, and its arches look lit from within.
feed.lookAt: Look at the colour contrast: warm floodlights on old stone against a deep blue dusk sky. Shoot in the short window after sunset, when the sky still holds colour but the lights are on. Stitching several frames, as here, lets a standard lens capture a monument this wide.

feed.title: East Banqueting House and St James's, Chipping Campden

image.credit: Saffron Blaze, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Chipping Campden is a market town in the Cotswold district of Gloucestershire, England, notable for its terraced High Street, which dates from the 14th to the 17th centuries. It was a wool trading centre in the Middle Ages and enjoyed the patronage of wealthy wool merchants, most notably William Greville, who died in 1401. Its buildings are made of locally quarried oolitic limestone known as Cotswold stone. Saffron Blaze photographed the gate and East Banqueting House of Campden Court beside the tower of St James's Church on 1 April 2012, under a clear blue sky.
feed.lookAt: Look at the stone: the honey-coloured limestone of the banqueting house and the church tower match, so the two read as one place. A green foreground and a blue sky make a simple three-band frame. Pair the building with the tower behind it to show how the town fits together.

caption.title: East Banqueting House and St James's, Chipping Campden

feed.title: Congress and Theatre House, Bad Ischl

image.credit: P e z i, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Bad Ischl is a spa town in the south of Upper Austria, on the river Traun in the centre of the Salzkammergut region. It is the home of the Kaiservilla, the summer residence of the Austro-Hungarian monarchs Emperor Franz Joseph I and Empress Elisabeth. In 2024 it was one of the European Capitals of Culture, the third Austrian city after Graz and Linz. The photographer P e z i took this view of the congress and theatre building on 19 July 2014. A fountain plays in the middle of a formal garden, with flower beds in front and a tall curved roof behind.
feed.lookAt: Look at the symmetry: the fountain sits on the central axis of the building, with the steps and the flower beds mirroring left and right. Stand on that axis, keep the camera level and let the foreground planting add colour at the bottom edge of a formal, balanced frame.

caption.title: Congress and Theatre House, Bad Ischl
caption.line2: P e z i · Upper Austria

feed.title: James H. Clark Center at dusk

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The James H. Clark Center, usually called the Clark Center, is a building at Stanford University in California, United States. It was completed in 2003 and houses interdisciplinary research in the biological sciences. King of Hearts photographed its courtyard on 24 October 2019 at 18:50 in the evening, and made an HDR image from three exposures ranging from +2 to −2, which keeps detail in both the lit interiors and the darkening sky. A round, stepped plaza fills the foreground, and the curved upper floors of the building wrap around it under a sweeping roof.
feed.lookAt: Look at the curves: the circular steps in the foreground echo the long curve of the roof and the balconies. A wide lens low to the ground exaggerates them. At dusk, when interior lights match the sky, bracketing several exposures keeps both the glowing windows and the deep blue.

caption.title: James H. Clark Center at dusk

feed.title: Town hall of Großbottwar

image.credit: Felix König (original), Papa Lima Whiskey (edit), CC BY 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Großbottwar is a town in the Ludwigsburg district of Baden-Württemberg, Germany, on a tourist route through the Württemberg wine region. The town was founded in the mid-13th century by an alliance of prominent families. Unlike most towns in the region, it was neither heavily damaged by war nor by urban fires, so many buildings from the 15th to 17th centuries survive with their original timber framing. The 16th-century Rathaus, or town hall, is noted for its half-timber construction and decoratively carved facade. Felix König photographed it on 30 October 2010, and Papa Lima Whiskey made the edited version used here.
feed.lookAt: Look at the pattern: red timber framing against pale plaster forms a repeating web of triangles and diagonals. Keep the camera level and the verticals straight, as in this tall frame, so that the gable stays symmetrical, and let the cobbled street in the foreground lead the eye upward.

feed.title: The Calanques of Piana, Corsica

image.credit: Myrabella, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Piana is a commune in the Corse-du-Sud department of France, on the island of Corsica. It is a member of Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, the association of the Most Beautiful Villages of France. The file page for this picture, taken by Myrabella on 19 August 2013, calls the rock formations around it the Calanques of Piana. In the frame, jagged red-orange rock towers rise on the left and right of a narrow gap, tinted with green pines, and a road cuts across the slope below. The sky overhead is clear and an intense blue.
feed.lookAt: Look at the colour split: orange rock against pure blue sky needs no editing to look bold. Use the V-shaped gap between the two rock masses as a natural frame, and shoot when the sun is high and the sky is clear so the rock stays saturated.

feed.title: Winter dawn above the clouds on Ai-Petri

image.credit: Dmytro Balkhovitin, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Ai-Petri is a peak in the Crimean Mountains, within the Yalta municipality for administrative purposes. Its name is of Greek origin and means St. Peter. Dmytro Balkhovitin photographed this panorama of the winter dawn on 1 March 2014 at about 06:35. Low clouds fill the valley below the summit like a sea, and the sun comes up under a thin band of cloud on the horizon. Frost covers the rocks and a lone pine in the foreground, while a dark stack of rock stands against the glowing sky, and the cloud bank stretches to the far horizon.
feed.lookAt: Look at the layers: frosted rock in front, a bank of cloud in the middle, a glowing horizon behind. Climb above the cloud before sunrise, and expose for the sky so the foreground rocks become dark silhouettes with a bright rim of frost along their edges.

caption.title: Winter dawn above the clouds on Ai-Petri

feed.title: Pembroke College Hall, Oxford

image.credit: Godot13, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Pembroke College is a constituent college of the University of Oxford, on Pembroke Square in Oxford. King James I of England and VI of Scotland founded it in 1624, using in part the endowment of the merchant Thomas Tesdale, and it was named after William Herbert, 3rd Earl of Pembroke, who was then Lord Chamberlain and Chancellor of the University. Like many Oxford colleges, it admitted only men until 1979. Godot13 photographed the Hall in the Chapel Quad on 15 April 2014. The stone building stands behind a striped lawn, its tall windows catching sunlight under a clear sky.
feed.lookAt: Look at the lawn: the mown stripes lead straight to the building and make the foreground part of the picture. Shoot college quads in clear sun, with the camera low and the lens wide, so the stone stays warm and the sky stays a deep, uncluttered blue.

feed.title: Garden shed at Wildenberg Castle, Zernez

image.credit: Agnes Monkelbaan, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Planta-Wildenberg Castle is a castle in the municipality of Zernez, in the Canton of Graubünden, Switzerland. It is a Swiss heritage site of national significance. Agnes Monkelbaan photographed the garden shed in the inner garden on 20 September 2023, in the afternoon. The little building has a steep, tiled roof topped with a small finial, and green-painted wooden walls decorated with yellow-cream patterns, including a repeated flower shape. Behind it, a steep slope covered in dark conifer forest fills the frame, and the late-summer leaves of nearby shrubs frame its left side.
feed.lookAt: Look at the contrast: a small, bright green building against a huge dark forest. A plain, dark background makes the colours and patterns of a small subject stand out. Step back and use the trees as a backdrop, then let leaves at the edge frame the shot.

facts: Swiss heritage site of national significance

caption.title: Garden shed at Wildenberg Castle, Zernez

feed.title: Going am Wilden Kaiser in winter

image.credit: Bernie Kohl, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Going am Wilden Kaiser is a municipality in the district of Kitzbühel in the Austrian region of Sölllandl, 8.5 km northwest of Kitzbühel. It has 1,849 inhabitants, divided into five sub-districts, and its main source of income is tourism. The Astbergbahn chairlift takes skiers from the village up to the Ski Welt skiing area. Bernie Kohl made this panorama on 29 January 2011, looking north across about 167 degrees. Snow lies deep over the roofs and meadows of the village, and the white crags of the Wilder Kaiser stand along the skyline under a blue sky.
feed.lookAt: Look at the proportions: the extremely wide, shallow frame lets the long ridge dominate while the church tower and snow-covered roofs sit low in the picture. A panorama needs a clear horizontal subject; stitch overlapping frames with the camera level to keep the skyline straight.

caption.title: Going am Wilden Kaiser in winter

feed.title: Wilkin River near the Makarora confluence

image.credit: Michal Klajban, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Wilkin River is a river in the Otago region of New Zealand, flowing into Lake Wānaka. It was named after Robert Wilkin, one of the early pastoral runholders in the Wānaka district, and it lies within Mount Aspiring National Park. Michal Klajban photographed the river close to its confluence with the Makarora River, on the South Island, on 4 April 2019. Still, shallow water mirrors the hillside on the far bank, where a row of tall, pale poplar-like trees stands out against dark green slopes, and the ridges of the mountains fade into soft cloud behind.
feed.lookAt: Look at the reflection: still water doubles the hillside and the trees, so the picture splits into two matching halves. Set the horizon of the bank near the middle, and wait for a calm moment so that the surface mirrors the tall trees cleanly.

caption.title: Wilkin River near the Makarora confluence

feed.title: Kursalon Hübner at dusk, Vienna

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Kursalon Hübner is a music hall in the Stadtpark in Vienna, Austria. It was designed by Johann Garben in the style of the Italian Renaissance and built between 1865 and 1867. Diego Delso photographed it on 31 January 2020 at 18:09, in the evening, and made an HDR image. The warm lights under the arcades glow against the cool twilight sky. Statues stand along the roofline, a green-domed pavilion closes each end, and the paving in the foreground leads straight to the steps at the centre, so the whole scene feels ordered and calm.
feed.lookAt: Look at the lamps and arches: warm points of light repeat along the arcade while the sky stays cool blue. Shoot in the twenty minutes after sunset and centre the building on a straight, symmetrical axis; the paving then leads the eye to the entrance.

feed.title: Tekniska verken headquarters at Stångebro, Linköping

image.credit: tomhe, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Linköping is a city in southern Sweden, the seat of Linköping Municipality and the capital of Östergötland County, with around 167,000 inhabitants in 2024. It lies on the Östergötland Plain and is known for its cathedral, its university and its high-technology industry. The photographer tomhe took this picture of the headquarters of Tekniska verken at Stångebro on 21 April 2006. The long building and an older brick structure stand beside still water. Bare trees rise against a heavy, dramatic cloud, and the whole scene is reflected in the surface below it.
feed.lookAt: Look at the reflection: calm water repeats the building, the bare trees and the cloud, making a second picture in the lower half. Choose a windless evening, set the horizon in the middle of the frame, and let the dramatic cloud carry the mood.

feed.title: Viborg Katedralskole in the morning

image.credit: Slaunger, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Viborg Katedralskole is a public gymnasium, or secondary school, and an IB World School in Viborg, Denmark. It stands at Gammel Skivevej 2 and supports about 1,000 students. Slaunger photographed the eastern facade as a morning panorama on 12 April 2015, at about 09:17. The long building has a symmetrical front with a central pediment, red tiled roofs and a small tower, and it rises behind a stone terrace and a wide, empty green field. A football goal stands on the grass in the foreground, and bare trees frame both sides.
feed.lookAt: Look at the symmetry: the school's centre line splits the frame into mirror halves, and the flat green pitch in front gives it room. A panorama of a long facade works best from a distance, level and dead centre, in early sun that lights the whole front evenly.

feed.title: Fields near Julio Andrade, Carchi

image.credit: Diego Delso, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Carchi is a province in Ecuador whose capital is Tulcán. The Carchi River rises on the slopes of Chiles volcano and forms the boundary between Colombia and Ecuador near Tulcán, and the Rumichaca Bridge is the most important land route between the two countries. Diego Delso photographed this view of the fields from Julio Andrade on 21 July 2015. Patchwork farmland in many shades of green rolls over low hills, with scattered trees and farm buildings, and wide, bright clouds fill much of the sky above the valley and the distant ridges.
feed.lookAt: Look at the patchwork: fields of different greens form shapes that guide the eye across the hills. A high viewpoint turns farmland into graphic pattern. Wait for cloud shadows to move across the slopes, because patches of light and shade add depth to a wide panorama.

feed.title: Adam Thoroughgood House, Virginia Beach

image.credit: PumpkinSky, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The Thoroughgood House is a brick house at 1636 Parish Road in Virginia Beach, Virginia, United States, built about 1719. It was formerly known as the Adam Thoroughgood House, but it was not built by Adam. It was restored in 1923 and again in the 1950s, and has served as a museum since opening to the public on 29 April 1957. The City of Virginia Beach acquired the property in 2003, and the house reopened in May 2011 after a restoration. PumpkinSky photographed the south side on 10 September 2017: tall brick chimneys, small diamond-paned windows and green trees all around.
feed.lookAt: Look at the chimney: the stepped brick end wall is the strongest shape here, so shoot it at an angle that shows two sides at once. Soft shade under the trees keeps the brick colour rich, while a small patch of blue sky above holds the corner of the frame.

feed.title: California State Capitol dome, Sacramento

image.credit: Radomianin, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: The California State Capitol is the seat of California's state government, in Sacramento. It houses the chambers of the State Legislature, made up of the Assembly and the Senate, and the office of the governor. The Neoclassical building was designed by Reuben S. Clark and built between 1861 and 1874. It stands at the west end of Capitol Park and was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1973. Radomianin photographed the pediment, rotunda and dome from the northwest on 20 March 2024 at 15:33. White stone and statues stand out against a deep blue sky, with flags flying on the mast in front.
feed.lookAt: Look at the angle: pointing up from close to the wall makes the dome tower over the pediment, while a deep blue sky isolates the white stone. Use a polarising filter or a high-sun afternoon to darken the sky, and put the flagpole on the centre line.

feed.title: Silver Lake at first light, Mono County

image.credit: King of Hearts, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

feed.story: Silver Lake is a lake within the Inyo National Forest in Mono County, California, in the United States. A public U.S. Forest Service campground is on its bank, and Silver Lake Resort, which offers simple facilities for travelers, is close by. The lake is fed by Rush Creek. King of Hearts photographed it on 6 September 2016 at about 06:47, early in the morning. The first sun lights the highest peak in orange while the lake below stays in cool shadow, and the still water reflects the mountains and carries the same orange glow on its surface.
feed.lookAt: Look at the light: the peak catches the sun while the valley is still dark, so the orange rock is the brightest thing in the frame. Arrive before sunrise, expose for the lit summit and use foreground boulders as a base, so the mirrored water doubles the picture.
